1	=== page 1 ===
2	AID: Efﬁcient Prediction of Aggregated Intensity of
3	Dependency in Large-scale Cloud Systems
4	Tianyi Yang∗, Jiacheng Shen∗, Yuxin Su∗, Xiao Ling†, Yongqiang Yang†, and Michael R. Lyu∗
5	∗Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China.
6	Email:{tyyang, jcshen, yxsu, lyu}@cse.cuhk.edu.hk
7	†Computing and Networking Innovation Lab, Cloud BU, Huawei
8	Email:{lingxiao1, yangyongqiang}@huawei.com
9	Abstract—Service reliability is one of the key challenges that
10	cloud providers have to deal with. In cloud systems, unplanned
11	service failures may cause severe cascading impacts on their de-
12	pendent services, deteriorating customer satisfaction. Predicting
13	the cascading impacts accurately and efﬁciently is critical to the
14	operation and maintenance of cloud systems. Existing approaches
15	identify whether one service depends on another via distributed
16	tracing but no prior work focused on discriminating to what
17	extent the dependency between cloud services is. In this paper,
18	we survey the outages and the procedure for failure diagnosis in
19	two cloud providers to motivate the deﬁnition of the intensity of
20	dependency. We deﬁne the intensity of dependency between two
21	services as how much the status of the callee service inﬂuences
22	the caller service. Then we propose AID, the ﬁrst approach to
23	predict the intensity of dependencies between cloud services. AID
24	ﬁrst generates a set of candidate dependency pairs from the
25	spans. AID then represents the status of each cloud service with
26	a multivariate time series aggregated from the spans. With the
27	representation of services, AID calculates the similarities between
28	the statuses of the caller and the callee of each candidate pair.
29	Finally, AID aggregates the similarities to produce a uniﬁed value
30	as the intensity of the dependency. We evaluate AID on the
31	data collected from an open-source microservice benchmark and
32	a cloud system in production. The experimental results show
33	that AID can efﬁciently and accurately predict the intensity
34	of dependencies. We further demonstrate the usefulness of our
35	method in a large-scale commercial cloud system.
36	Index Terms —cloud computing, software reliability, AIOps,
37	service dependency
38	I. I NTRODUCTION
39	Service reliability is one of the key challenges that cloud
40	providers have to deal with. The common practice nowadays
41	is developing and deploying small, independent, and loosely
42	coupled cloud microservices that collectively serve users’
43	requests. The microservices that serve the same purpose are
44	called cloud services 1. The microservices communicate with
45	each other through well-deﬁned APIs. Such an architecture
46	is called microservice architecture [1]. The microservice ar-
47	chitecture has been widely adopted in cloud systems because
48	of its reliability and ﬂexibility. Under this architecture, mi-
49	croservice management frameworks like Kubernetes will be
50	responsible for managing the life cycles of microservices.
51	Yuxin Su is the corresponding author.
52	1For simplicity, in this paper, “cloud service” and “cloud microservice” are
53	interchangeable when they are used alone.
54	Developers can focus on the application logic instead of the
55	bothering tasks of resource management and failure recovery.
56	Although microservice management frameworks provide
57	automatic mechanisms for failure recovery, unplanned service
58	failures may still cause severe cascading effects. For example,
59	failures of critical services that provide basic request routing
60	functions will impact the invocation of cloud services, slow
61	down request processing, and deteriorate customer satisfaction.
62	Therefore, evaluating the impact of service failures rapidly
63	and accurately is critical to the operation and maintenance
64	of cloud systems. Knowing the scope of the impact, reliability
65	engineers can put more emphasis on services that have greater
66	impacts on others.
67	A failed service will only affect services that will invoke
68	it. In other words, service invocations cause dependencies
69	between services. Many recent approaches [2], [3] propose
70	to use the dependencies of services to approximate their
71	failure impact. All the services and dependencies in a cloud
72	system collectively construct a directed graph of services,
73	which is also called a dependency graph. Identifying whether
74	one service depends on another in cloud systems can be
75	well solved by industrial tracing frameworks like Dapper and
76	Jaeger. By using these frameworks, all the invocations between
77	the caller and callee services can be recorded as traces that are
78	composed of spans. The attributes about each invocation, like
79	duration, status, invoked service name, timestamp, etc., are
80	recorded in each span. Based on the spans, current dependency
81	detection methods treat the dependency as a binary value
82	indicating whether one service invokes another or not.
83	However, modeling the relations of services solely with
84	binary dependencies is not precise enough. To show the insufﬁ-
85	ciency of existing methods, we ﬁrst conduct an empirical study
86	on the outages of Amazon Web Service and Huawei Cloud.
87	We point out that it is inefﬁcient to conduct failure diagnosis
88	and recovery based on binary dependencies. This is because
89	the different dependencies of a cloud service impact the cloud
90	service in different ways. Manual examination of different
91	dependencies without any priority is inefﬁcient, especially in
92	cloud systems where the number of dependencies could be
93	large. Based on this observation, we argue that it will be help-
94	ful if the dependency can be measured as a continuous value
95	that indicates the intensity of this dependency. Speciﬁcally,
96	by checking services that are dependent on the failed service
97	arXiv:2109.04893v1  [cs.SE]  20 Aug 2021
98	=== page 2 ===
99	with large intensity values, on-call engineers (OCEs) can ﬁnd
100	the root cause of a system failure with a higher probability.
101	By recovering the services that are strongly dependent on the
102	failed one, the whole system could be restored faster.
103	To improve the reliability of cloud systems, in this paper, we
104	propose AID, an end-to-end approach to predict the intensity
105	of dependencies between cloud microservices for cascading
106	failure prediction. We ﬁrst generate a set of candidate depen-
107	dency pairs from the spans. Then we distribute each span into
108	different ﬁxed-length bins according to their timestamp and
109	service name. We calculate the statistics of all spans in each
110	bin as the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for the bin. The
111	KPIs of one service form a multivariate time series that will
112	be treated as the representation of the service’s status. For
113	each candidate dependency pair, we calculate the similarities
114	between the statuses of the two services in the pair. Finally,
115	we aggregate the similarities to produce a uniﬁed value as the
116	intensity of the pair.
117	To show the effectiveness of AID, we evaluate AID on
118	two datasets. One is a simulated dataset, and the other is an
119	industrial dataset. For the simulated dataset, we deploy train-
120	ticket, an open-source microservice benchmark system, simu-
121	late users’ requests, and collect the traces. For the industrial
122	dataset, we collect the traces from a production cloud system.
123	Then we evaluate AID on the datasets and compare its perfor-
124	mance with several baselines. The experimental results show
125	that our proposed method can accurately measure the intensity
126	of dependencies and outperform the baselines. Furthermore,
127	we showcase the successful usage of our method in a large-
128	scale production cloud system. In addition, we release both
129	datasets to facilitate future studies.
130	The main contributions of this work are highlighted as
131	follows:
132	• We propose AID, the ﬁrst method to quantify the intensity
133	of dependencies between different services.
134	• The evaluation results show the effectiveness and efﬁ-
135	ciency of the proposed method.
136	• We release a simulated dataset and an industrial dataset
137	from a production cloud system to facilitate future stud-
138	ies.
139	Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as
140	follows. Section II provides motivation and background knowl-
141	edge that underpin our approach. We describe our survey and
142	empirical study on real outages that motivate the proposed
143	method in Section III. Section IV elaborates on the method
144	in detail. Section V introduces the datasets, baselines and
145	shows the experimental results. Successful use cases of the
146	proposed method in a production cloud system are demon-
147	strated in Section VI. We discuss the practical usage, the
148	perceived limitations, and the possible threats to validity in
149	Section VII. Section VIII introduces related works. The last
150	section, Section IX, concludes this paper and lists directions
151	for future exploration.
152	II. B ACKGROUND
153	In this section, we brieﬂy describe the service-oriented
154	architecture of cloud systems and the distributed tracing tools
155	in cloud systems. Then we present the main techniques, i.e.,
156	time series similarity analysis, that underpin our approach.
157	A. The Architecture of Cloud Systems
158	Modern cloud systems are often constructed from a complex
159	and large-scale hierarchy of distributed software modules [4].
160	The common practice nowadays is to develop and deploy these
161	software modules as cloud microservices that collectively
162	comprise multiple large cloud services [5]. Microservices are
163	small, independent, and loosely coupled software modules that
164	can be deployed independently [1]. Different microservices
165	serve different responsibilities [6] like user authentication,
166	resource allocation, virtual network management, billing, etc.
167	When an external request arrives at the cloud system, the
168	request will be routed through the system and served by dozens
169	of different cloud services and microservices. The microser-
170	vices communicate with each other through well-deﬁned APIs
171	and, therefore, can be refactored and scaled independently and
172	dynamically to adapt to incidents like surges of requests and
173	service failures [7]. Such an architecture is called microservice
174	architecture [1].
175	The microservice architecture becomes increasingly popular
176	due to its high ﬂexibility, reusability, and scalability [8]. It en-
177	ables agile development and supports polyglot programming,
178	i.e., microservices developed under different technical stacks
179	can work together smoothly. However, the loosely coupled
180	nature of microservices makes it difﬁcult for engineers to
181	conduct system maintenance. Different microservices in a
182	large cloud system are usually developed and managed by
183	separate teams. Each team only has access to their own
184	services as well as services that are closely related, which
185	means they only have a local view of the whole system [9].
186	As a result, the failure diagnosis, fault localization, and
187	performance debugging in a large cloud system become more
188	complex than ever [10]–[12]. Despite various fault tolerance
189	mechanisms introduced by modern cloud systems, it is still
190	possible for minor anomalies to magnify their impact and
191	escalate into system outages. As exempliﬁed in Section III-A,
192	when a cloud service enters an anomalous state and does not
193	return results in a timely manner, other services that depend
194	on it will also suffer from the increased request latency. Such
195	anomalous states can propagate through the service-calling
196	structure and eventually affect the entire system, resulting in
197	a degraded user experience or even a service outage.
198	B. Distributed Tracing
199	For commercial cloud providers, it is crucial to troubleshoot
200	and ﬁx the failures in a timely manner because massive
201	user applications may be affected even by a small service
202	failure [13]. Distributed tracing is a crucial technique for
203	gaining insight and observability to cloud systems.
204	In large-scale cloud systems, a request is usually handled
205	by multiple chained service invocations. As clues to defective
206	=== page 3 ===
207	Span 0
208	Span 1 Span 2 Span 3
209	Span 4 Span 5

211	Fig. 1. A trace log with six spans.
212	services are hidden in the intricate network of services, it
213	is difﬁcult for even knowledgeable OCEs to keep track of
214	how a request is processed in the cloud system. Distributed
215	tracing provides an approach to monitor the execution path
216	of each request. For chained service invocations, e.g., service
217	A invokes service B, and service B invokes service C, it
218	is important to know the status of each service invocation,
219	including the result, the duration of execution, etc. By adding
220	hooks to the services and microservices of the cloud system, a
221	distributed tracing system [14]–[16] can record the contextual
222	information of each service invocation. Such records are called
223	span logs, abbreviated as spans. A span represents a logical
224	unit of execution that is handled by a microservice in a
225	cloud system. All the spans that serve for the same request
226	collectively form a directed graph of spans, as illustrated in
227	Figure 1. Such a directed graph of spans generated by a request
228	is called a piece of trace log, abbreviated as a trace. A trace
229	represents an execution path through the cloud system. With a
230	trace, engineers can track how the request propagates through
231	the cloud system. Collectively analyzing the traces of the
232	entire cloud system can help engineers obtain in-depth latency
233	reports that could assist failure diagnosis, fault localization,
234	and surface performance degradation in the cloud system.

272	C. Time Series Similarity Analysis
273	Time series data are ubiquitous. One important task in time
274	series data mining is to measure the similarity between two
275	time series. Similar to human intuition, the similarity measure
276	is usually based on the similarity between the shapes of two
277	time series [19].
278	Dynamic time warping (DTW) [20] is a widely-used sim-
279	ilarity measure when two time series have the same overall
280	component shapes but are not aligned on the timeline. It
281	attempts to align two time series along a timeline by distorting
282	the timeline for one time series so that its converted form is
283	better aligned with the second time series. DTW was initially
284	used in speech recognition applications [20] and extended and
285	optimized by many works [21]–[23].
286	III. M OTIVATIONS
287	The research described in this paper is motivated by the
288	maintenance of a real-world cloud system in production. In
289	this section, we ﬁrst survey thirteen publicly known service
290	outages that severely affected Amazon Web Services (AWS)
291	from 2011 to 2020. Among the thirteen outages, we identify
292	ﬁve that are related to service dependency and summarized the
293	consequences of inappropriate management of service depen-
294	dency. Second, we empirically study the diagnosis records of
295	ﬁve real outages in the cloud system of Huawei Cloud that are
296	related to inappropriate management of service dependency.
297	Our study indicates that the information in the traces has not
298	been used efﬁciently and current practice heavily relies on the
299	engineers’ familiarity with the dependencies in the system.
300	Lastly, we propose to measure the intensity of dependency in
301	terms of status propagation between dependent cloud services.
302	We demonstrate the usefulness of the intensity by motivating
303	examples in real cloud systems.
304	A. A Survey of the Outages in AWS
305	Service outages are inevitable in the cloud [24]. In this sec-
306	tion, we empirically analyzed over 1000 incidents of Huawei
307	Cloud in 2019 and thirteen publicly known major outages 3 of
308	AWS from 2011 to 2020. Among the incidents of Huawei
309	Cloud, we found that improper service dependency is the
310	most frequent reason for failures in Huawei Cloud. Among
311	the outage summaries of AWS, we also identiﬁed that ﬁve

329	AWS is the worldwide leading cloud provider. It operates
330	in many regions, each consisting of multiple Availability
331	Zones (AZs). Each AZ uses separate physical facilities and
332	independently provides various cloud services [5], including
333	Steam Data Processing (Kinesis), API Usage Analysis (Cog-
334	nito), Customer Dashboard (Cloudwatch), Elastic Compute

336	Balancing (ELB), and Low-level Block Storage (EBS), etc. For
337	brevity’s sake, we simplify the dependencies as 1) EC2, RDS,
338	and ELB all depend on EBS, and 2) Cognito and Cloudwatch
339	depend on Kinesis 5.

341	both caused by erroneous upgrades of EBS. When EBS failed,
342	the services that depend on EBS, i.e., EC2,ELB, and RDS,
343	are all affected. The cascading failures resulted in service
344	disruptions of over 48 hours in the US-East-1 Region of AWS.
345	The outages on June 29, 2012, and August 7, 2014, are
346	both triggered by the blackouts. After the blackout, the RDS
347	and ELB services restarted quickly as expected, but they are
348	still unable to fully recover because they both depend on EBS
349	service which, at that time, can not recover simultaneously.
350	The slow failure recovery incurred by service dependencies
351	affected the service availability for days in the US-East-1
352	Region and the EU West-1 Region of AWS. As a follow-up
353	optimization, ELB service reduced the dependency on EBS
354	after the outage in 2014.
355	On November, 25 2020, the erroneous upgrade of Kinesis
356	lead to its failure, cascadingly causing the failure of Cognito
357	and Cloudwatch. More severely, during the recovery, AWS
358	could not notify the customers via the normal way because the
359	normal customer notiﬁcation service also relied on Cognito.
360	Due to the inner mechanism of Kinesis, the recovery of Kinesis
361	took more than ten hours. Thus the recoveries of Cognito
362	4The outages are usually caused by various reasons that mutually affect
363	each other. Service dependency is one of the reasons, so we use the word
364	“related”.
365	5The actual dependency relations between these services are complicated.
366	We omit the details here.
367	and Cloudwatch were also slowed down. As a follow-up
368	optimization, Cognito and Cloudwatch services reduced the
369	dependency on Kinesis after the severe outage.
370	B. Drawbacks of Current Failure Diagnosis Methods
371	To gain more knowledge about the procedure of failure
372	diagnosis in industrial circumstances, we ﬁrst interviewed en-
373	gineers in Huawei Cloud 6. Then we summarize the procedure
374	of failure diagnosis, and point out the drawbacks of current
375	practice in Huawei Cloud.
376	In Huawei Cloud, the failure diagnosis can be triggered
377	by two systems, i.e., the customer support system and the
378	monitoring system. When a customer experiences a service
379	disruption, the customer can submit a support ticket in the
380	customer support system. The on-call engineers will distribute
381	the support ticket to the corresponding engineers responsible
382	for the service. The monitoring system, on the other hand,
383	monitors the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and the logs
384	of each service in the cloud system. If the KPIs or the number
385	of erroneous logs of one service increased abnormally or
386	reached predeﬁned thresholds, the monitoring system will send
387	an alert to the corresponding engineers. Upon receiving the
388	support ticket or alert, engineers start diagnosing the failures.
389	We summarize the common practice of failure diagnosis
390	in Huawei Cloud as follows. Suppose the anomalous service
391	is A, OCEs will ﬁrst check whether the failure is caused by
392	the faults of service A (e.g., an erroneous upgrade). If so,
393	the development team of service A will handle the failure. If
394	service A is in good condition, OCEs will analyze the status
395	of all services that A depends on. The status includes the
396	number of calls, the error rate, etc. If they found the failure
397	of a service B is likely to cause the failure of service A, then
398	engineers will continue to investigate service B. Recall that
399	all the services construct a directed graph where each node
400	represents a service. The failure diagnosis procedure can be
401	viewed as a recursive search on the service dependency graph.
402	The practice works well in small cloud systems that con-
403	tain tens of cloud services. However, the dependencies in
404	large-scale cloud systems are much more complicated [10],
405	making manual failure diagnosis inefﬁcient and difﬁcult for
406	engineers. Engineers may have trouble identifying the cause
407	of the failure. In this case, the development teams of all
408	cloud services have to check whether the failure is caused by
409	their corresponding services. Sometimes engineers may infer
410	the possible causes of a failure, but it heavily relies on the
411	engineer’s familiarity with the dependencies in the system.
412	In summary, the complex dependency relations in large-scale
413	cloud systems make failure diagnosis difﬁcult, and current
414	practice is inefﬁcient and dependent on the human experience.
415	C. Intensity of Service Dependency
416	A cloud system is composed of many services. The depen-
417	dency between two services is caused by one service invoking
418	the other via predeﬁned APIs. Existing tools [2], [25], [26]

476	IV. A PPROACH
477	In this section, we present AID, a framework for predicting
478	the A ggregated I ntensity of service D ependency in large-
479	scale cloud systems. We ﬁrst present the overall workﬂow of
480	AID. Then we elaborate on each step in detail, i.e., candidate
481	selection, service status generation, and intensity prediction.
482	A. Overview
483	The overall workﬂow of AID is illustrated in Figure 4. AID
484	consists of three steps: candidate selection, status generation,
485	and intensity prediction. Given the raw traces, AID ﬁrst
486	generates a set of candidate service pairs (P,C ) where service
487	P directly invokes service C (Section IV-B). The intuition
488	is that direct service invocation incurs direct dependency to
489	some degree. Indirect dependencies through the transitivity
490	of service invocation will be discussed in Section VII-A.
491	For status generation, we generate the status of all ser-
492	vices (Section IV-C). The status of one service is composed
493	of three aspects of dependency, i.e., number of invocations,
494	duration of invocations, error of invocations. Each aspect of
495	the service’s status contains one or more Key Performance
496	Indicators (KPIs), depending on the actual implementation of
497	the distributed tracing system. A KPI is an aggregated value
498	of a service status of all the spans of a service in a ﬁxed
499	time interval, e.g., 1 minute. We use the statistical indicators
500	of each aggregation as the values of the KPIs. Motivated by
501	the experience of engineers introduced in Section III-B, we
502	propose to predict the intensity of service dependencies from
503	the similarity of the statuses of dependent services. The intu-
504	ition behind using the similarity of time series is to evaluate
505	the propagation of service statuses. The intensity prediction
506	step (Section IV-D) predicts the intensity of dependency by
507	measuring the similarity between two service’s statuses. The
508	similarity between two service’s statuses is a normalized and
509	weighted average of the similarity of all the KPIs of the two
510	services. We calculate the similarity between two KPIs by a
511	dynamic status warping algorithm. Finally, AID produces the
512	dependency graph with intensity.
513	B. Candidate Selection

515	two categories, i.e., synchronous invocations and asynchronous
516	invocations. Modern tracing mechanisms can keep track of
517	both synchronous and asynchronous invocations [28]. Given

563	C. Service Status Generation
564	In this step, we generate the status of all cloud services from
565	the traces. We start by deﬁning the status of a cloud service
566	(i.e., service status) and then describe the procedure of service
567	status generation.
568	Deﬁnition of Service Status: A service invocation is com-
569	posed of three logical components, i.e., the caller service, the
570	callee service, and the network communication. In particular,
571	the caller service initiates an invocation to the callee service
572	via the network. The callee service then processes the invo-
573	cation, during which it may invoke other services. After the
574	processing is ﬁnished, the callee service will send the result,
575	e.g., status, to the caller service via the network. Hence, we
576	could derive three aspects of service invocations: initiation
577	of invocation, processing, result. As service invocations occur
578	repeatedly, the three aspects of service invocations can derive
579	three aspects of service dependency:
580	• Number of Invocations : The number of invocations from
581	the caller to the callee,
582	• Duration of Invocations : The duration of invocations,
583	• Error of Invocations: The number of successful invoca-
584	tions from the caller to the callee.
585	Representation of Service Status: In a cloud system, the
586	spans record information about every invocation. Intuitively,
587	the status of a cloud service can be easily obtained from the
588	spans of that service. Inspired by the common practice in
589	cloud monitoring [29], we distribute the spans of one service
590	into many bins according to the spans’ timestamps. Each bin
591	accepts spans whose timestamp is in a short, ﬁxed-length
592	period. We denote the length of the short period as τ. For
593	example, the span shown in Figure 2 will be put in the bin of
594	ts-preserve-service at time 04:58, April 17 2020. We
595	can then represent the status of a cloud service in a short
596	period by the statistical indicators of all the spans in the
597	corresponding bin.

599	periodT , we ﬁrst initiate S× N empty bins of the predeﬁned

613	wheret is the time of the bin and M is the microservice name
614	of the bin. If a service is not invoked in a particular bin (i.e.,

617	t. Ordering the bins by t, we get three time series of KPIs for
618	each cloud service, denoted as invoM , errM , and durM . We
619	name the time series of server KPIs as status series.
620	D. Intensity Prediction

=== page 1 ===
AID: Efﬁcient Prediction of Aggregated Intensity of
Dependency in Large-scale Cloud Systems
Tianyi Yang∗, Jiacheng Shen∗, Yuxin Su∗, Xiao Ling†, Yongqiang Yang†, and Michael R. Lyu∗
∗Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China.
Email:{tyyang, jcshen, yxsu, lyu}@cse.cuhk.edu.hk
†Computing and Networking Innovation Lab, Cloud BU, Huawei
Email:{lingxiao1, yangyongqiang}@huawei.com
Abstract—Service reliability is one of the key challenges that
cloud providers have to deal with. In cloud systems, unplanned
service failures may cause severe cascading impacts on their de-
pendent services, deteriorating customer satisfaction. Predicting
the cascading impacts accurately and efﬁciently is critical to the
operation and maintenance of cloud systems. Existing approaches
identify whether one service depends on another via distributed
tracing but no prior work focused on discriminating to what
extent the dependency between cloud services is. In this paper,
we survey the outages and the procedure for failure diagnosis in
two cloud providers to motivate the deﬁnition of the intensity of
dependency. We deﬁne the intensity of dependency between two
services as how much the status of the callee service inﬂuences
the caller service. Then we propose AID, the ﬁrst approach to
predict the intensity of dependencies between cloud services. AID
ﬁrst generates a set of candidate dependency pairs from the
spans. AID then represents the status of each cloud service with
a multivariate time series aggregated from the spans. With the
representation of services, AID calculates the similarities between
the statuses of the caller and the callee of each candidate pair.
Finally, AID aggregates the similarities to produce a uniﬁed value
as the intensity of the dependency. We evaluate AID on the
data collected from an open-source microservice benchmark and
a cloud system in production. The experimental results show
that AID can efﬁciently and accurately predict the intensity
of dependencies. We further demonstrate the usefulness of our
method in a large-scale commercial cloud system.
Index Terms —cloud computing, software reliability, AIOps,
service dependency
I. I NTRODUCTION
Service reliability is one of the key challenges that cloud
providers have to deal with. The common practice nowadays
is developing and deploying small, independent, and loosely
coupled cloud microservices that collectively serve users’
requests. The microservices that serve the same purpose are
called cloud services 1. The microservices communicate with
each other through well-deﬁned APIs. Such an architecture
is called microservice architecture [1]. The microservice ar-
chitecture has been widely adopted in cloud systems because
of its reliability and ﬂexibility. Under this architecture, mi-
croservice management frameworks like Kubernetes will be
responsible for managing the life cycles of microservices.
Yuxin Su is the corresponding author.
1For simplicity, in this paper, “cloud service” and “cloud microservice” are
interchangeable when they are used alone.
Developers can focus on the application logic instead of the
bothering tasks of resource management and failure recovery.
Although microservice management frameworks provide
automatic mechanisms for failure recovery, unplanned service
failures may still cause severe cascading effects. For example,
failures of critical services that provide basic request routing
functions will impact the invocation of cloud services, slow
down request processing, and deteriorate customer satisfaction.
Therefore, evaluating the impact of service failures rapidly
and accurately is critical to the operation and maintenance
of cloud systems. Knowing the scope of the impact, reliability
engineers can put more emphasis on services that have greater
impacts on others.
A failed service will only affect services that will invoke
it. In other words, service invocations cause dependencies
between services. Many recent approaches [2], [3] propose
to use the dependencies of services to approximate their
failure impact. All the services and dependencies in a cloud
system collectively construct a directed graph of services,
which is also called a dependency graph. Identifying whether
one service depends on another in cloud systems can be
well solved by industrial tracing frameworks like Dapper and
Jaeger. By using these frameworks, all the invocations between
the caller and callee services can be recorded as traces that are
composed of spans. The attributes about each invocation, like
duration, status, invoked service name, timestamp, etc., are
recorded in each span. Based on the spans, current dependency
detection methods treat the dependency as a binary value
indicating whether one service invokes another or not.
However, modeling the relations of services solely with
binary dependencies is not precise enough. To show the insufﬁ-
ciency of existing methods, we ﬁrst conduct an empirical study
on the outages of Amazon Web Service and Huawei Cloud.
We point out that it is inefﬁcient to conduct failure diagnosis
and recovery based on binary dependencies. This is because
the different dependencies of a cloud service impact the cloud
service in different ways. Manual examination of different
dependencies without any priority is inefﬁcient, especially in
cloud systems where the number of dependencies could be
large. Based on this observation, we argue that it will be help-
ful if the dependency can be measured as a continuous value
that indicates the intensity of this dependency. Speciﬁcally,
by checking services that are dependent on the failed service
arXiv:2109.04893v1  [cs.SE]  20 Aug 2021
=== page 2 ===
with large intensity values, on-call engineers (OCEs) can ﬁnd
the root cause of a system failure with a higher probability.
By recovering the services that are strongly dependent on the
failed one, the whole system could be restored faster.
To improve the reliability of cloud systems, in this paper, we
propose AID, an end-to-end approach to predict the intensity
of dependencies between cloud microservices for cascading
failure prediction. We ﬁrst generate a set of candidate depen-
dency pairs from the spans. Then we distribute each span into
different ﬁxed-length bins according to their timestamp and
service name. We calculate the statistics of all spans in each
bin as the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for the bin. The
KPIs of one service form a multivariate time series that will
be treated as the representation of the service’s status. For
each candidate dependency pair, we calculate the similarities
between the statuses of the two services in the pair. Finally,
we aggregate the similarities to produce a uniﬁed value as the
intensity of the pair.
To show the effectiveness of AID, we evaluate AID on
two datasets. One is a simulated dataset, and the other is an
industrial dataset. For the simulated dataset, we deploy train-
ticket, an open-source microservice benchmark system, simu-
late users’ requests, and collect the traces. For the industrial
dataset, we collect the traces from a production cloud system.
Then we evaluate AID on the datasets and compare its perfor-
mance with several baselines. The experimental results show
that our proposed method can accurately measure the intensity
of dependencies and outperform the baselines. Furthermore,
we showcase the successful usage of our method in a large-
scale production cloud system. In addition, we release both
datasets to facilitate future studies.
The main contributions of this work are highlighted as
follows:
• We propose AID, the ﬁrst method to quantify the intensity
of dependencies between different services.
• The evaluation results show the effectiveness and efﬁ-
ciency of the proposed method.
• We release a simulated dataset and an industrial dataset
from a production cloud system to facilitate future stud-
ies.
Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as
follows. Section II provides motivation and background knowl-
edge that underpin our approach. We describe our survey and
empirical study on real outages that motivate the proposed
method in Section III. Section IV elaborates on the method
in detail. Section V introduces the datasets, baselines and
shows the experimental results. Successful use cases of the
proposed method in a production cloud system are demon-
strated in Section VI. We discuss the practical usage, the
perceived limitations, and the possible threats to validity in
Section VII. Section VIII introduces related works. The last
section, Section IX, concludes this paper and lists directions
for future exploration.
II. B ACKGROUND
In this section, we brieﬂy describe the service-oriented
architecture of cloud systems and the distributed tracing tools
in cloud systems. Then we present the main techniques, i.e.,
time series similarity analysis, that underpin our approach.
A. The Architecture of Cloud Systems
Modern cloud systems are often constructed from a complex
and large-scale hierarchy of distributed software modules [4].
The common practice nowadays is to develop and deploy these
software modules as cloud microservices that collectively
comprise multiple large cloud services [5]. Microservices are
small, independent, and loosely coupled software modules that
can be deployed independently [1]. Different microservices
serve different responsibilities [6] like user authentication,
resource allocation, virtual network management, billing, etc.
When an external request arrives at the cloud system, the
request will be routed through the system and served by dozens
of different cloud services and microservices. The microser-
vices communicate with each other through well-deﬁned APIs
and, therefore, can be refactored and scaled independently and
dynamically to adapt to incidents like surges of requests and
service failures [7]. Such an architecture is called microservice
architecture [1].
The microservice architecture becomes increasingly popular
due to its high ﬂexibility, reusability, and scalability [8]. It en-
ables agile development and supports polyglot programming,
i.e., microservices developed under different technical stacks
can work together smoothly. However, the loosely coupled
nature of microservices makes it difﬁcult for engineers to
conduct system maintenance. Different microservices in a
large cloud system are usually developed and managed by
separate teams. Each team only has access to their own
services as well as services that are closely related, which
means they only have a local view of the whole system [9].
As a result, the failure diagnosis, fault localization, and
performance debugging in a large cloud system become more
complex than ever [10]–[12]. Despite various fault tolerance
mechanisms introduced by modern cloud systems, it is still
possible for minor anomalies to magnify their impact and
escalate into system outages. As exempliﬁed in Section III-A,
when a cloud service enters an anomalous state and does not
return results in a timely manner, other services that depend
on it will also suffer from the increased request latency. Such
anomalous states can propagate through the service-calling
structure and eventually affect the entire system, resulting in
a degraded user experience or even a service outage.
B. Distributed Tracing
For commercial cloud providers, it is crucial to troubleshoot
and ﬁx the failures in a timely manner because massive
user applications may be affected even by a small service
failure [13]. Distributed tracing is a crucial technique for
gaining insight and observability to cloud systems.
In large-scale cloud systems, a request is usually handled
by multiple chained service invocations. As clues to defective

C. Time Series Similarity Analysis
Time series data are ubiquitous. One important task in time
series data mining is to measure the similarity between two
time series. Similar to human intuition, the similarity measure
is usually based on the similarity between the shapes of two
time series [19].
Dynamic time warping (DTW) [20] is a widely-used sim-
ilarity measure when two time series have the same overall
component shapes but are not aligned on the timeline. It
attempts to align two time series along a timeline by distorting
the timeline for one time series so that its converted form is
better aligned with the second time series. DTW was initially
used in speech recognition applications [20] and extended and
optimized by many works [21]–[23].
III. M OTIVATIONS
The research described in this paper is motivated by the
maintenance of a real-world cloud system in production. In
this section, we ﬁrst survey thirteen publicly known service
outages that severely affected Amazon Web Services (AWS)
from 2011 to 2020. Among the thirteen outages, we identify
ﬁve that are related to service dependency and summarized the
consequences of inappropriate management of service depen-
dency. Second, we empirically study the diagnosis records of
ﬁve real outages in the cloud system of Huawei Cloud that are
related to inappropriate management of service dependency.
Our study indicates that the information in the traces has not
been used efﬁciently and current practice heavily relies on the
engineers’ familiarity with the dependencies in the system.
Lastly, we propose to measure the intensity of dependency in
terms of status propagation between dependent cloud services.
We demonstrate the usefulness of the intensity by motivating
examples in real cloud systems.

B. Drawbacks of Current Failure Diagnosis Methods
To gain more knowledge about the procedure of failure
diagnosis in industrial circumstances, we ﬁrst interviewed en-
gineers in Huawei Cloud 6. Then we summarize the procedure
of failure diagnosis, and point out the drawbacks of current
practice in Huawei Cloud.
In Huawei Cloud, the failure diagnosis can be triggered
by two systems, i.e., the customer support system and the
monitoring system. When a customer experiences a service
disruption, the customer can submit a support ticket in the
customer support system. The on-call engineers will distribute
the support ticket to the corresponding engineers responsible
for the service. The monitoring system, on the other hand,
monitors the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and the logs
of each service in the cloud system. If the KPIs or the number
of erroneous logs of one service increased abnormally or
reached predeﬁned thresholds, the monitoring system will send
an alert to the corresponding engineers. Upon receiving the
support ticket or alert, engineers start diagnosing the failures.
We summarize the common practice of failure diagnosis
in Huawei Cloud as follows. Suppose the anomalous service
is A, OCEs will ﬁrst check whether the failure is caused by
the faults of service A (e.g., an erroneous upgrade). If so,
the development team of service A will handle the failure. If
service A is in good condition, OCEs will analyze the status
of all services that A depends on. The status includes the
number of calls, the error rate, etc. If they found the failure
of a service B is likely to cause the failure of service A, then
engineers will continue to investigate service B. Recall that
all the services construct a directed graph where each node
represents a service. The failure diagnosis procedure can be
viewed as a recursive search on the service dependency graph.
The practice works well in small cloud systems that con-
tain tens of cloud services. However, the dependencies in
large-scale cloud systems are much more complicated [10],
making manual failure diagnosis inefﬁcient and difﬁcult for
engineers. Engineers may have trouble identifying the cause
of the failure. In this case, the development teams of all
cloud services have to check whether the failure is caused by
their corresponding services. Sometimes engineers may infer
the possible causes of a failure, but it heavily relies on the
engineer’s familiarity with the dependencies in the system.
In summary, the complex dependency relations in large-scale
cloud systems make failure diagnosis difﬁcult, and current
practice is inefﬁcient and dependent on the human experience.

IV. A PPROACH
In this section, we present AID, a framework for predicting
the A ggregated I ntensity of service D ependency in large-
scale cloud systems. We ﬁrst present the overall workﬂow of
AID. Then we elaborate on each step in detail, i.e., candidate
selection, service status generation, and intensity prediction.
A. Overview
The overall workﬂow of AID is illustrated in Figure 4. AID
consists of three steps: candidate selection, status generation,
and intensity prediction. Given the raw traces, AID ﬁrst
generates a set of candidate service pairs (P,C ) where service
P directly invokes service C (Section IV-B). The intuition
is that direct service invocation incurs direct dependency to
some degree. Indirect dependencies through the transitivity
of service invocation will be discussed in Section VII-A.
For status generation, we generate the status of all ser-
vices (Section IV-C). The status of one service is composed
of three aspects of dependency, i.e., number of invocations,
duration of invocations, error of invocations. Each aspect of
the service’s status contains one or more Key Performance
Indicators (KPIs), depending on the actual implementation of
the distributed tracing system. A KPI is an aggregated value
of a service status of all the spans of a service in a ﬁxed
time interval, e.g., 1 minute. We use the statistical indicators
of each aggregation as the values of the KPIs. Motivated by
the experience of engineers introduced in Section III-B, we
propose to predict the intensity of service dependencies from
the similarity of the statuses of dependent services. The intu-
ition behind using the similarity of time series is to evaluate
the propagation of service statuses. The intensity prediction
step (Section IV-D) predicts the intensity of dependency by
measuring the similarity between two service’s statuses. The
similarity between two service’s statuses is a normalized and
weighted average of the similarity of all the KPIs of the two
services. We calculate the similarity between two KPIs by a
dynamic status warping algorithm. Finally, AID produces the
dependency graph with intensity.
B. Candidate Selection
In general, direct service invocations can be divided into
two categories, i.e., synchronous invocations and asynchronous
invocations. Modern tracing mechanisms can keep track of
both synchronous and asynchronous invocations [28]. Given
all the raw traces of the cloud system, in this step, we
generate a candidate dependency set Cand. The candi-
date dependency set Cand contains service invocation pairs
(P1,C 1), (P2,C 2),··· , (Pn,Cn). Each pair (Pi,Ci) in the
candidate dependency set denotes that the service named

C. Service Status Generation
In this step, we generate the status of all cloud services from
the traces. We start by deﬁning the status of a cloud service
(i.e., service status) and then describe the procedure of service
status generation.
Deﬁnition of Service Status: A service invocation is com-
posed of three logical components, i.e., the caller service, the
callee service, and the network communication. In particular,
the caller service initiates an invocation to the callee service
via the network. The callee service then processes the invo-
cation, during which it may invoke other services. After the
processing is ﬁnished, the callee service will send the result,
e.g., status, to the caller service via the network. Hence, we
could derive three aspects of service invocations: initiation
of invocation, processing, result. As service invocations occur
repeatedly, the three aspects of service invocations can derive
three aspects of service dependency:
• Number of Invocations : The number of invocations from
the caller to the callee,
• Duration of Invocations : The duration of invocations,
• Error of Invocations: The number of successful invoca-
tions from the caller to the callee.
Representation of Service Status: In a cloud system, the
spans record information about every invocation. Intuitively,
the status of a cloud service can be easily obtained from the
spans of that service. Inspired by the common practice in
cloud monitoring [29], we distribute the spans of one service
into many bins according to the spans’ timestamps. Each bin
accepts spans whose timestamp is in a short, ﬁxed-length
period. We denote the length of the short period as τ. For
example, the span shown in Figure 2 will be put in the bin of
ts-preserve-service at time 04:58, April 17 2020. We
can then represent the status of a cloud service in a short
period by the statistical indicators of all the spans in the
corresponding bin.
Formally, given all the spans in the cloud system over a long
periodT , we ﬁrst initiate S× N empty bins of the predeﬁned
size τ. S is the number of microservices. N, determined by

D. Intensity Prediction
In this paper, we deﬁne the intensity of dependency between
two services as how much the status of the callee service
inﬂuences the status of the caller service . The step of intensity
prediction quantitatively predicts the intensity of dependency
by measuring the similarity between two services’ status
series. Speciﬁcally, we calculate the similarity of two different
status series with dynamic status warping and aggregate all the
similarities to get the overall similarity.

the maximum duration of the callee’s spans plus δrtt.

synchronization in cloud systems, so we add an undirected

945	E. RQ4: How efﬁcient is AID?
946	The most time-consuming operations are the candidate
947	selection and service status generation steps because we have
948	to iterate over all the spans in the cloud system. Theoretically,
949	the time complexities of the candidate selection and service
950	status generation steps are O(S), where S is the number of
951	spans to process in the cloud system. In practice, the industrial
952	dataset contains about 1.0× 1010 spans, so we process it
953	with a distributed computing service in Huawei Cloud. Since
954	the preprocessing is dynamically scheduled and mixed with
955	other teams’ tasks, we do not count the time spent on it. For
956	the intensity prediction step, the time complexity is O(kN 2),
957	where N = T
958	τ is the number of bins and k is proportional
959	to the warping window w. In practice, the intensity prediction
960	step takes 155 seconds on average to process two status series
961	both with 1440 bins on a laptop. Since the similarity calcula-
962	tion of different (P,C ) pairs are independent, we could easily
963	parallelize the intensity prediction step to further improve the
964	time efﬁciency.
965	VI. C ASE STUDY
966	In Huawei Cloud, AID has been successfully incorporated
967	into the dependency management system that serves hundreds

970	dates the aggregated intensity in the dependency management
971	system. The reliability engineers will categorize the intensity
972	into different levels by referring to both the output of AID
973	and their domain expertise. Then the dependency management
974	system will provide reference to the engineers in optimizing
975	dependencies and mitigating cascading failures.

1021	VII. D ISCUSSION
1022	A. Practical Usage and Perceived Limitations
1023	1) Indirect Dependencies: In this work, we mainly consid-
1024	ered direct dependencies, which is caused by direct service in-
1025	vocations. The proposed approach does not explicitly consider
1026	indirect dependencies through transitivity of service invocation
1027	because the intensity of indirect dependencies can be easily
1028	inferred from direct dependencies. In practice, the intensity
1029	of indirect dependencies can be inferred by a “cascading
1030	conduction mechanism” that if A intensively depends on B
1031	and B intensively depends on C then A intensively depends on
1032	C. The proposed approach also works well on dependencies
1033	caused by circuit breakers as long as the circuit breakers work
1034	transparently.
1035	2) Extension of Service Status: In this paper, we only derive
1036	three aspects of service invocations, i.e., number of invoca-
1037	tions, duration of invocations, error of invocations. We utilized
1038	them because they are part of the state-of-the-art tracing
1039	system. Other aspects like the content of invocation responses
1040	can also be important to determine status. In practice, cloud
1041	providers can incorporate additional information to extend the
1042	representation of service status in their own implementation
1043	of AID.
1044	3) Limitations on Asynchronous Invocations: Although
1045	modern tracing mechanisms can keep track of asynchronous
1046	invocations, AID may suffer from inaccuracies when dealing
1047	with asynchronous invocations. This is because the max time
1048	drift δd in Algorithm 1 is hard to estimate for asynchronous
1049	service invocations. Furthermore, if the traces of synchronous
1050	and asynchronous invocations are mixed, AID may not work
1051	well since the time drift of synchronous and asynchronous
1052	invocations usually differs a lot. We leave this problem as
1053	future work.
1054	B. Threat to Validity
1055	In this work, we identiﬁed the following major threats to
1056	validity.
1057	1) Labeling accuracy: In this paper, we propose to measure
1058	the intensity of service dependency with AID. To evaluate
1059	the practical usage of AID, we conduct experiments on a
1060	simulated dataset and an industrial dataset. As it is a new
1061	relation between cloud services, manual labeling is needed
1062	for the evaluation. The evaluation on the industrial dataset
1063	requires engineers to manually inspect the dependencies and
1064	label the intensity of dependencies. Limited by the experience
1065	of engineers, the label may not be 100% accurate. The
1066	fast evolution of cloud services may also change their fault
1067	tolerance mechanism, resulting in inaccurate labels. However,
1068	the engineers we invited have rich domain knowledge and
1069	are in charge of the architecture design of the cloud system
1070	of Huawei Cloud. They also discuss with each other when
1071	there are disagreements. Moreover, the labeled dependencies
1072	are the core cloud services in Huawei Cloud, so the intensity
1073	of dependencies are stable during the data collection period.
1074	We believe the amount of inaccurate labels is small (if exists).
1075	Most importantly, our method is unsupervised, so inaccurate
1076	labels will not affect the prediction results of the proposed
1077	method.
1078	2) Insufﬁciency of the simulation: For the evaluation pur-
1079	pose, we deploy an open-source microservice benchmark to
1080	simulate a real cloud system. The benchmark only contains
1081	25 microservices, which is far below the number of cloud
1082	microservices in a real cloud. Additionally, the implementation
1083	of the open-source benchmark did not fully consider the
1084	fault tolerance, resulting in only one weak dependency in the
1085	simulation. Hence, the simulated dataset may not exhibit some
1086	common attributes of a real cloud system. For example, the
1087	proportion of “strong” dependency in the simulated dataset is
1088	twice the proportion of “strong” dependency in the industrial
1089	dataset. However, the insufﬁciency of the simulation will
1090	not hinder the practical usefulness of AID in the real cloud
1091	system. On the contrary, as we show in Section V, the
1092	proposed method works better on the industrial dataset. The
1093	experimental results on the simulated dataset only conﬁrm the
1094	insufﬁciency of the simulation.

1096	VIII. R ELATED WORK
1097	A. Cloud Monitoring
1098	Monitoring cloud services properly with low overhead is
1099	the key to provide reliable services. Distributed Tracing, as
1100	a means of monitoring distributed cloud services, has been
1101	widely studied in the literature. All the distributed tracing
1102	approaches can be classiﬁed as intrusive tracing and non-
1103	intrusive tracing. Intrusive tracing requires modiﬁcation to
1104	application code either in run time or at compile time. Google
1105	proposes Dapper [14] to help engineers understand system
1106	behavior and reasoning about performance issues. It reduces
1107	the tracing overhead by sampling and restricting the instru-
1108	mentation number. X-Trace [16] monitors and reconstructs the
1109	whole request path from a client by modifying all the network
1110	protocols and embedding the tracing data to the package
1111	header.
1112	Non-intrusive tracing approaches do not require code mod-
1113	iﬁcation and usually have a lower overhead. Normally, these
1114	approaches leverage information like the system runtime logs
1115	and the source code to reconstruct the real event traces. Zhao
1116	et. al. [31] propose lprof to reconstruct the execution ﬂow of
1117	distributed systems using the runtime log of these systems.
1118	lprof conducts static analysis on the call-graph of request
1119	processing code of the system to attribute a log output to a
1120	client request. Chow et. al. [32] also leverage system runtime
1121	logs to conduct performance monitoring and analysis. They
1122	propose ¨UberTrace to reconstruct traces from the existing logs,
1123	then use The Mystery Machine to construct a causal model
1124	and conduct analyses. Stitch uses pattern matching on logs to
1125	reconstruct the hierarchical relationship of events in a system.
1126	Pensieve [33] automatically reconstructs a chain of causally
1127	dependent events that leads to a system failure exploiting the
1128	log ﬁles and system bytecode.
1129	B. Dependency Mining
1130	Automatically discovering service dependencies is critical to
1131	cloud system administration and maintenance. There are two
1132	major types of dependency mining approaches, i.e., passive
1133	dependency mining and active ones. Passive dependency min-
1134	ing generates service dependency based purely on the runtime
1135	logs or KPIs. Shah et. al. [34] propose to use Recurrent
1136	Neural Networks (RNNs) to analyze and extract dependencies
1137	in KPIs and use the discovered dependencies to identify early
1138	indicators for a given performance metric, analyze lagged
1139	and temporal dependencies, and to improve forecast accuracy.
1140	EIDefrawy et. al. [35] use Transfer Entropy to passively mine
1141	the dependencies. Luo et. al. [25] apply log parsing and
1142	Bayesian decision theory to estimate the direction of depen-
1143	dencies among services. They employ time delay consistency
1144	to reduce false dependencies. Zand et. al. [36] construct a
1145	service correlation graph based on network measures and
1146	extract dependencies using hypothesis-testing. They further
1147	compute an importance metric for network’s components
1148	to facilitate administration. CloudScout [3] employs Pearson
1149	Product-moment Correction Coefﬁcient over machine-level
1150	KPIs such as TCP/UDP connection numbers and CPU uti-
1151	lization to calculate the similarity between different services.
1152	The similarity measure is used to cluster different services
1153	together and to conduct VM consolidation based on the service
1154	clusters. Unlike all these approaches that mostly use physical
1155	machine metrics to infer service dependencies, our method
1156	is designed for the emerging microservice architecture and
1157	utilizes the trace logs that directly record service invocations.
1158	Active dependency mining requires modiﬁcation to ser-
1159	vices. Ma et. al. propose GMAT [2], which generates service
1160	dependencies in the microservice architecture leveraging the
1161	reﬂection feature of Java and visualizes the dependencies to
1162	engineers. Rippler [26] extracts the dependencies by randomly
1163	injecting temporal perturbation patterns in request arrival tim-
1164	ings for different services and investigates the propagation of
1165	the patterns. Wang et. al. [37] constructs a service knowledge
1166	graph using real-time measures, operational metadata, and
1167	business features. They propose new metrics to measure the
1168	popularity of services based on their dependencies. Novotny
1169	et. al. [38] focus on mining dependencies on the highly
1170	dynamic mobile networks. They use local monitors to collect
1171	local views of dependencies and generate a global view of
1172	dependency on demand.
1173	IX. C ONCLUSION
1174	In this paper, we ﬁrst conduct a comprehensive empirical
1175	study on the maintenance of AWS and Huawei Cloud. We
1176	identify the inefﬁciency in failure diagnosis and recovery
1177	with the binary-valued dependencies and deﬁne the intensity
1178	of dependency for the ﬁrst time. To facilitate cloud main-
1179	tenance, we propose AID, the ﬁrst approach to predict the
1180	intensity of dependencies between cloud microservices. AID
1181	ﬁrst generates a set of candidate dependency pairs from the
1182	spans. AID then represents the status of each cloud service
1183	with a multivariate time series aggregated from the spans and
1184	calculates the similarities between the statuses of the caller
1185	and callee of each candidate pair. Finally, AID aggregate the
1186	similarities to produce a uniﬁed value as the intensity of the
1187	dependency. For the evaluation, we collect and manually label
1188	a new dataset from an open-source microservice benchmark
1189	and evaluate AID on it. Furthermore, we evaluate AID using
1190	the data of Huawei Cloud and showcase the practical usage
1191	of AID. Both the evaluation results and case studies show the
1192	efﬁciency and effectiveness of AID. In the future, we plan to
1193	incorporate more information from the traces and other service
1194	logs for more accurate predictions.

V. E XPERIMENTS
In this section, we evaluate AID on both a simulated dataset
and an industrial dataset. Particularly, we aim to answer the
following research questions (RQs):
• RQ1. How effective is AID in predicting the intensity of
dependency?
• RQ2. What is the impact of different parameter settings?
• RQ3. What is the impact of different similarity measures?
• RQ4. How efﬁcient is AID?
A. Experimental Setup
1) Dataset: To show the practical effectiveness of AID, we
further conduct experiments on the simulated dataset and an
industrial dataset from the cloud system of Huawei Cloud.
Since there are no existing datasets of trace logs, we deploy
a benchmark microservice system to simulate a real cloud
system. We simulate user requests and collect the generated
trace logs to construct the simulated dataset. We release both
datasets with the paper to facilitate future studies in this ﬁeld 8.
Simulated dataset : For the simulated dataset, we deploy
train-ticket [18], an open-source microservice benchmark, for
data collection. Train-ticket is a web-based ticketing system
with 25 microservices, through which users can search for

tickets, reserve tickets, and pay for the reserved tickets. An
open-source tracing framework, Jaeger, is used to trace all the
API calls. To generate traces, we develop a request simulator
that simulates normal users’ access to the ticketing system. The
simulator will log in to the system, search for tickets, reserve
a ticket according to the results of the search, and pay for the
ticket. Then we collect the traces from Jaeger and transform
the traces into 17,471,024 spans. The dataset is termed as “TT”
in Table II.
Industrial dataset : Apart from the simulated dataset, we
also collected traces from a region of Huawei Cloud to
evaluate AID. To support tens of millions of users world-
wide, the cloud system of Huawei Cloud contains numerous
cloud services and microservices. The service invocations
are monitored and recorded by an independently developed
distributed tracing system. The complex dependency relations
in the cloud system increase the burden of OCEs. The OCEs
can diagnose problematic microservices timely if the intensity
of dependencies can be automatically detected in real-time. To
evaluate the practical effectiveness of our method, we collected
a 7-day-long trace dataset with 192 microservices in April
2021. The dataset is termed as “Industry” in Table II.
Manual labeling: Since our method is unsupervised, labels
are only for evaluation. Neither of the datasets has labels about
the intensity of dependency, so manual labeling is needed.
We set two candidate labels for the intensity of dependency,
i.e., “strong” and “weak”. Given a candidate dependency pair
(P,C ), if the failure of service C will cause the failure of
service P , the intensity between (P,C ) should be labeled
“strong”; otherwise it should be labeled “weak”. For the
simulated dataset, two Ph.D. students inspect the source code
of all microservices and label every service dependency inde-
pendently. For the industrial dataset, several senior engineers
are invited to manually label the intensity of dependency. In
both processes, disagreement on labels will be discussed until
consensus is reached. Finally, we convert the “strong” labels
to 1 and the “weak” labels to 0 so that they can be effectively
compared with the computed intensities.
The statistics of the datasets are listed in Table II. “#
Microservices” denotes the number of microservices in the
dataset. “# Spans” denotes the number of spans in the dataset.
“# Strong” and “# Weak” denote the number of dependencies
that are labeled with “strong” or “weak” respectively.
2) Baselines: Since there is no existing work that measures
the intensity of service dependency, we use Pearson correla-
tion coefﬁcient, Spearman correlation coefﬁcient, and Kendall
Rank correlation coefﬁcient as the baseline. Particularly, we
calculate correlation on the status series of a candidate depen-
dency pair (P,C ), denoted as corrp(P,C )
status and corrs(P,C )
status.
For the baselines, we directly use the implementation from the
Python package scipy. We map the correlation to [0, 1] with
the functionf (x) = (x+1)/2. The intensities of dependencies
are then produced in the same way as Equation 2.
3) Evaluation Metrics: We employ Cross Entropy (CE),
Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Squared Error

4) Experimental Environments: We run the experiments on

on the industrial dataset run on a Laptop with Intel Core i7
CPU @ 2.60 GHz and 16 GB RAM.
B. RQ1: How effective is AID in predicting the intensity of
dependency?
To study the effectiveness of AID, we compare its perfor-
mance with the baseline models on both the simulated dataset
and the industrial dataset collected from Huawei Cloud. For
the parameters of AID, we set the bin size τ = 1 minute,
the estimated round trip time δrtt = 0 . Specially, we set the
max time drift δd = 1 minute for the industrial dataset and
set δd = 0 for the simulated dataset. We do this because the
simulated dataset is deployed in a single server, so the time
drift will not be a problem. In addition, we use moving average
to smoothen the status series for the baselines and our method.
The outputs are scalar values ranging from 0 to 1. A larger
value indicates higher intensity. The overall performance is
shown in Table III, where we mark the smallest loss for each
loss metric and dataset.
=== page 9 ===
AID achieves the best performance on the industrial dataset
and reduces the loss by 45.8%, 61.1%, and 33.2% in terms
of cross entropy, mean absolute error, and root mean squared
error. On the simulated dataset, AID achieves the best per-
formance in terms of cross entropy and root mean squared
error. Pearson correlation coefﬁcient marginally outperforms
AID on the simulated dataset. The improvement of AID on the
simulated dataset is smaller than that on the industrial dataset.
This is because the benchmark for simulation did incorporate
very few fault tolerance mechanisms, making most of the
dependencies strong. Moreover, since the service invocations
of the TT benchmark are very fast, the statuses of TT’s
services are relatively similar, making simple baselines and
our approach perform similarly.

E. RQ4: How efﬁcient is AID?
The most time-consuming operations are the candidate
selection and service status generation steps because we have
to iterate over all the spans in the cloud system. Theoretically,
the time complexities of the candidate selection and service
status generation steps are O(S), where S is the number of
spans to process in the cloud system. In practice, the industrial
dataset contains about 1.0× 1010 spans, so we process it
with a distributed computing service in Huawei Cloud. Since
the preprocessing is dynamically scheduled and mixed with
other teams’ tasks, we do not count the time spent on it. For
the intensity prediction step, the time complexity is O(kN 2),
where N = T
τ is the number of bins and k is proportional
to the warping window w. In practice, the intensity prediction
step takes 155 seconds on average to process two status series
both with 1440 bins on a laptop. Since the similarity calcula-
tion of different (P,C ) pairs are independent, we could easily
parallelize the intensity prediction step to further improve the
time efﬁciency.
VI. C ASE STUDY
In Huawei Cloud, AID has been successfully incorporated
into the dependency management system that serves hundreds
to thousands of cloud services. Figure 6 illustrates the concep-
tual workﬂow. AID processes trace logs and continuously up-
dates the aggregated intensity in the dependency management
system. The reliability engineers will categorize the intensity
into different levels by referring to both the output of AID
and their domain expertise. Then the dependency management
system will provide reference to the engineers in optimizing
dependencies and mitigating cascading failures.
A. Optimization of Dependencies
In a cloud system, service failures are inevitable, but we can
prevent the failures from affecting other services by optimizing

improper dependencies. AID assists in the discovery of unnec-
essary strong dependency on critical cloud services. If a critical
cloud service depends on another service with high intensity,
the dependency management system will remind the engineers
to check whether the dependency is necessary. If the depen-
dency is unnecessary, the development team has to reduce the
intensity of the dependency to improve the robustness of the
critical cloud service. Since AID’s deployment, more than ten
unnecessary dependencies of critical cloud services have been
discovered by AID and optimized by the development team.
B. Mitigation of Cascading Failures
AID also assists in the mitigation of cascading failures.
During a cascading failure, AID can provide the latest intensity
of dependency to OCEs, so that they can diagnose service
failures efﬁciently. In addition, when a cascading failure
occurs, OCEs can limit the trafﬁc to critical cloud services and
recover the dependencies marked as “strong” ﬁrst. By doing
so, the service disruption can get under control. Once a critical
failure occurs, the manually conﬁrmed “strong” dependencies
will be treated with high priority. We conduct ﬁeld interviews
with OCEs to collect feedback. Based on the feedback, we
have seen our method shedding light on reducing the impact
of critical failures.
VII. D ISCUSSION
A. Practical Usage and Perceived Limitations
1) Indirect Dependencies: In this work, we mainly consid-
ered direct dependencies, which is caused by direct service in-
vocations. The proposed approach does not explicitly consider
indirect dependencies through transitivity of service invocation
because the intensity of indirect dependencies can be easily
inferred from direct dependencies. In practice, the intensity
of indirect dependencies can be inferred by a “cascading
conduction mechanism” that if A intensively depends on B
and B intensively depends on C then A intensively depends on
C. The proposed approach also works well on dependencies
caused by circuit breakers as long as the circuit breakers work
transparently.
2) Extension of Service Status: In this paper, we only derive
three aspects of service invocations, i.e., number of invoca-
tions, duration of invocations, error of invocations. We utilized
them because they are part of the state-of-the-art tracing
system. Other aspects like the content of invocation responses
can also be important to determine status. In practice, cloud
providers can incorporate additional information to extend the
representation of service status in their own implementation
of AID.
3) Limitations on Asynchronous Invocations: Although
modern tracing mechanisms can keep track of asynchronous
invocations, AID may suffer from inaccuracies when dealing
with asynchronous invocations. This is because the max time
drift δd in Algorithm 1 is hard to estimate for asynchronous
service invocations. Furthermore, if the traces of synchronous
and asynchronous invocations are mixed, AID may not work
well since the time drift of synchronous and asynchronous
invocations usually differs a lot. We leave this problem as
future work.
B. Threat to Validity
In this work, we identiﬁed the following major threats to
validity.
1) Labeling accuracy: In this paper, we propose to measure
the intensity of service dependency with AID. To evaluate
the practical usage of AID, we conduct experiments on a
simulated dataset and an industrial dataset. As it is a new
relation between cloud services, manual labeling is needed
for the evaluation. The evaluation on the industrial dataset
requires engineers to manually inspect the dependencies and
label the intensity of dependencies. Limited by the experience
of engineers, the label may not be 100% accurate. The
fast evolution of cloud services may also change their fault
tolerance mechanism, resulting in inaccurate labels. However,
the engineers we invited have rich domain knowledge and
are in charge of the architecture design of the cloud system
of Huawei Cloud. They also discuss with each other when
there are disagreements. Moreover, the labeled dependencies
are the core cloud services in Huawei Cloud, so the intensity
of dependencies are stable during the data collection period.
We believe the amount of inaccurate labels is small (if exists).
Most importantly, our method is unsupervised, so inaccurate
labels will not affect the prediction results of the proposed
method.
2) Insufﬁciency of the simulation: For the evaluation pur-
pose, we deploy an open-source microservice benchmark to
simulate a real cloud system. The benchmark only contains
25 microservices, which is far below the number of cloud
microservices in a real cloud. Additionally, the implementation
of the open-source benchmark did not fully consider the
fault tolerance, resulting in only one weak dependency in the
simulation. Hence, the simulated dataset may not exhibit some
common attributes of a real cloud system. For example, the
proportion of “strong” dependency in the simulated dataset is
twice the proportion of “strong” dependency in the industrial
dataset. However, the insufﬁciency of the simulation will
not hinder the practical usefulness of AID in the real cloud
system. On the contrary, as we show in Section V, the
proposed method works better on the industrial dataset. The
experimental results on the simulated dataset only conﬁrm the
insufﬁciency of the simulation.

VIII. R ELATED WORK
A. Cloud Monitoring
Monitoring cloud services properly with low overhead is
the key to provide reliable services. Distributed Tracing, as
a means of monitoring distributed cloud services, has been
widely studied in the literature. All the distributed tracing
approaches can be classiﬁed as intrusive tracing and non-
intrusive tracing. Intrusive tracing requires modiﬁcation to
application code either in run time or at compile time. Google
proposes Dapper [14] to help engineers understand system
behavior and reasoning about performance issues. It reduces
the tracing overhead by sampling and restricting the instru-
mentation number. X-Trace [16] monitors and reconstructs the
whole request path from a client by modifying all the network
protocols and embedding the tracing data to the package
header.
Non-intrusive tracing approaches do not require code mod-
iﬁcation and usually have a lower overhead. Normally, these
approaches leverage information like the system runtime logs
and the source code to reconstruct the real event traces. Zhao
et. al. [31] propose lprof to reconstruct the execution ﬂow of
distributed systems using the runtime log of these systems.
lprof conducts static analysis on the call-graph of request
processing code of the system to attribute a log output to a
client request. Chow et. al. [32] also leverage system runtime
logs to conduct performance monitoring and analysis. They
propose ¨UberTrace to reconstruct traces from the existing logs,
then use The Mystery Machine to construct a causal model
and conduct analyses. Stitch uses pattern matching on logs to
reconstruct the hierarchical relationship of events in a system.
Pensieve [33] automatically reconstructs a chain of causally
dependent events that leads to a system failure exploiting the
log ﬁles and system bytecode.
B. Dependency Mining
Automatically discovering service dependencies is critical to
cloud system administration and maintenance. There are two
major types of dependency mining approaches, i.e., passive
dependency mining and active ones. Passive dependency min-
ing generates service dependency based purely on the runtime
logs or KPIs. Shah et. al. [34] propose to use Recurrent
Neural Networks (RNNs) to analyze and extract dependencies
in KPIs and use the discovered dependencies to identify early
indicators for a given performance metric, analyze lagged
and temporal dependencies, and to improve forecast accuracy.
EIDefrawy et. al. [35] use Transfer Entropy to passively mine
the dependencies. Luo et. al. [25] apply log parsing and
Bayesian decision theory to estimate the direction of depen-
dencies among services. They employ time delay consistency
to reduce false dependencies. Zand et. al. [36] construct a
service correlation graph based on network measures and
extract dependencies using hypothesis-testing. They further
compute an importance metric for network’s components
to facilitate administration. CloudScout [3] employs Pearson
Product-moment Correction Coefﬁcient over machine-level
KPIs such as TCP/UDP connection numbers and CPU uti-
lization to calculate the similarity between different services.
The similarity measure is used to cluster different services
together and to conduct VM consolidation based on the service
clusters. Unlike all these approaches that mostly use physical
machine metrics to infer service dependencies, our method
is designed for the emerging microservice architecture and
utilizes the trace logs that directly record service invocations.
Active dependency mining requires modiﬁcation to ser-
vices. Ma et. al. propose GMAT [2], which generates service
dependencies in the microservice architecture leveraging the
reﬂection feature of Java and visualizes the dependencies to
engineers. Rippler [26] extracts the dependencies by randomly
injecting temporal perturbation patterns in request arrival tim-
ings for different services and investigates the propagation of
the patterns. Wang et. al. [37] constructs a service knowledge
graph using real-time measures, operational metadata, and
business features. They propose new metrics to measure the
popularity of services based on their dependencies. Novotny
et. al. [38] focus on mining dependencies on the highly
dynamic mobile networks. They use local monitors to collect
local views of dependencies and generate a global view of
dependency on demand.
IX. C ONCLUSION
In this paper, we ﬁrst conduct a comprehensive empirical
study on the maintenance of AWS and Huawei Cloud. We
identify the inefﬁciency in failure diagnosis and recovery
with the binary-valued dependencies and deﬁne the intensity
of dependency for the ﬁrst time. To facilitate cloud main-
tenance, we propose AID, the ﬁrst approach to predict the
intensity of dependencies between cloud microservices. AID
ﬁrst generates a set of candidate dependency pairs from the
spans. AID then represents the status of each cloud service
with a multivariate time series aggregated from the spans and
calculates the similarities between the statuses of the caller
and callee of each candidate pair. Finally, AID aggregate the
similarities to produce a uniﬁed value as the intensity of the
dependency. For the evaluation, we collect and manually label
a new dataset from an open-source microservice benchmark
and evaluate AID on it. Furthermore, we evaluate AID using
the data of Huawei Cloud and showcase the practical usage
of AID. Both the evaluation results and case studies show the
efﬁciency and effectiveness of AID. In the future, we plan to
incorporate more information from the traces and other service
logs for more accurate predictions.
