# AID: Aggregated Intensity of Dependency (Yang et al., 2021, arXiv)

> Reading notes from the **full text** (`litdb/texts/tianyiyang...txt`). Page numbers are PDF pages. Figs 1-6 not inspected.

## 1. One-paragraph summary
AID estimates how strongly a caller depends on a callee. Spans are binned per service into three KPIs (invocation count, error rate, mean duration). Directed time warping (DSW) measures similarity between caller and callee series, min-max normalised and averaged over the three KPIs. Evaluated against 19 and 75 hand-labelled dependencies (strong/weak) on Train-Ticket and a Huawei Cloud region. It outputs edge weights; it does not forecast when or whether a failure will occur.

## 2. Problem and motivation
- Binary dependency graphs cannot tell engineers which dependencies matter during an outage (pp.1-5).
- Evidence: 5 of 13 public AWS outages (2011-2020) are "related" to service dependency (38%) (Table I p.4); an analysis of over 1000 Huawei Cloud incidents in 2019 where improper dependency was reportedly the most frequent cause, with no figures given (p.3); engineer interviews at one company (p.4). Evidence type: small anecdotal survey plus one company's statement.
- Real? Plausible; the numbers are too thin to cite as a rate.

## 3. Method
- Candidate pairs (P, C) from parent/child spans; status series (invo, err, dur) per 1-minute bin; DSW: directed warping window = max callee duration + round-trip estimate, plus time-drift allowance (Algorithm 1 p.7); intensity I = mean of three min-max normalised similarities (Eq 1-2 p.7).
- Complexity O(k N^2) per pair; 155 s per pair of 1440-bin series on a laptop (p.9).
- Assumptions: direct calls only; transitive strength by chaining (p.10); asynchronous calls are a stated weakness (p.10).

## 4. Data and experimental setup
- TT: 25 services, 18 strong and 1 weak labels (Table II p.7). Industry: 192 services, 67 strong and 8 weak (Table II); only dependencies engineers knew were labelled (footnote p.7).
- Labels: two PhD students (TT) and senior engineers (Industry), consensus on disagreement.
- Parameters: bin 1 minute, round trip 0, drift 1 minute (Industry) or 0 (TT) (p.8). Bin sizes 1-10 minutes tested on Industry only.
- Leakage: none (unsupervised); but parameters are tuned on the evaluated data.

## 5. Results (copied)
| Metric | Theirs | Best baseline | Baseline name | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Industry CE / MAE / RMSE | 0.3270 / 0.1751 / 0.3044 | 0.6030 / 0.4501 / 0.4537 (best per column from Spearman) | correlation baselines | Table III p.8 |
| TT CE / MAE / RMSE | 0.4562 / 0.3435 / 0.3859 | 0.6464 (Kendall) / 0.3305 (Pearson) / 0.4388 (Pearson) | Pearson, Spearman, Kendall | Table III |
| DSW vs DTW on Industry | CE 0.3270 vs 0.3584 | n/a | AID_DTW | Table IV p.9 |
| Reduction on Industry | 45.8%, 61.1%, 33.2% (as stated) | n/a | n/a | p.9 |

- The 45.8% quoted for cross entropy matches 0.3270 vs 0.6030 (as reported). No statistical tests; one run.
- Case study: more than ten unnecessary dependencies found and optimised since deployment; engineer feedback only, no measured benefit (p.10).

## 6. Limitations
- Stated: labelling accuracy, small simulator with one weak dependency, asynchronous calls, indirect dependencies (pp.10).
- **My critique:**
  1. Task is dependency strength, not failure prediction; the "cascading failure prediction" framing is only motivation (p.2).
  2. Evaluation set is tiny and skewed: TT has 18 of 19 strong, so predicting "strong" everywhere scores well; Industry 67 of 75 strong (about 89%). A constant predictor of 0.89 would also be a natural baseline, not reported.
  3. Labels are binary and chosen by engineers for dependencies they knew; the continuous score is compared to 0/1.
  4. Baselines are correlation coefficients on the same series; no other dependency-mining methods (Rippler, CloudScout etc.) are run (p.11).
  5. Training-time and test-time parameters (drift, bin size) are set on the evaluation data.
  6. Stated "first": narrow claim (intensity from traces).
- Not discussed: label noise, confidence intervals, performance during an actual failure (the claimed cascading-failure use is anecdotal).

## 7. Reproducibility
- Code and data stated at github.com/OpsPAI/aid (not checked yet). Industrial data cannot be shared in full; the released set is described as released with the paper.

## 8. Comparison with OUR work
| Dimension | This paper | Ours (rca-lab) | Who is stronger, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Label requirement | none (labels for eval) | none | tie |
| Live / streaming | batch, anecdotal live use | incremental | ours (claimed) |
| Telemetry used | traces | traces (+ metrics) | similar |
| Propagation modelling | per-edge strength from time-warped similarity | learned edge probabilities | similar idea; theirs tested on edges |
| Forecasts future failures | no | claimed | n/a |
| Explanation | none | templates | ours |
| Evaluation rigor | 94 labelled edges, no CIs | synthetic | theirs has real data |
| Open / reproducible | stated | yes | tie |

- **What they have that we do not:** an evaluation of edge weights against engineer labels on a real cloud (Industry), and directed time-warping that handles caller-callee lag.
- **What we have that they do not:** use of the weights for RCA ranking and risk scoring; negative controls.
- **Could a reviewer say "this already exists"?** For "learn the strength of call edges from traces without labels": yes, partly. We must cite AID and compare our edge-weight estimator against its DSW similarity.
- **Position:** cite as prior work on label-free edge strength; do not call it failure prediction.
- **Must we run it as a baseline?** Yes, as a propagation-weight baseline if code is available.

## 9. Does this paper change what problem we should solve?
- It corrects my earlier reading of AID in `docs/REVIEW_REPORT.md` (it was described as predicting cascading impact; it estimates dependency strength). The gap "forecast cascade risk" is therefore less covered by AID than assumed, but "learn edge strength without labels" is covered.

## 10. Citation-ready facts (each with page)
- "AID derives a continuous dependency intensity from trace-derived invocation, error and duration series with a directed time-warping similarity" (pp.5-7).
- "On a Huawei Cloud region with 75 labelled dependencies, AID reached cross entropy 0.327 vs 0.603 for the best correlation baseline" (Table III p.8; note 67 of 75 labels are strong).

## 11. Open questions / things to verify
- Published venue; repo contents; whether AID's weights improve RCA ranking (not evaluated).

# AID: Aggregated Intensity of Dependency (Yang et al., 2021, arXiv)

> Reading notes from the **full text** (`litdb/texts/tianyiyang...txt`). Page numbers are PDF pages. Figs 1-6 not inspected.

## 1. One-paragraph summary
AID estimates how strongly a caller depends on a callee. Spans are binned per service into three KPIs (invocation count, error rate, mean duration). Directed time warping (DSW) measures similarity between caller and callee series, min-max normalised and averaged over the three KPIs. Evaluated against 19 and 75 hand-labelled dependencies (strong/weak) on Train-Ticket and a Huawei Cloud region. It outputs edge weights; it does not forecast when or whether a failure will occur.

## 2. Problem and motivation
- Binary dependency graphs cannot tell engineers which dependencies matter during an outage (pp.1-5).
- Evidence: 5 of 13 public AWS outages (2011-2020) are "related" to service dependency (38%) (Table I p.4); an analysis of over 1000 Huawei Cloud incidents in 2019 where improper dependency was reportedly the most frequent cause, with no figures given (p.3); engineer interviews at one company (p.4). Evidence type: small anecdotal survey plus one company's statement.
- Real? Plausible; the numbers are too thin to cite as a rate.

## 3. Method
- Candidate pairs (P, C) from parent/child spans; status series (invo, err, dur) per 1-minute bin; DSW: directed warping window = max callee duration + round-trip estimate, plus time-drift allowance (Algorithm 1 p.7); intensity I = mean of three min-max normalised similarities (Eq 1-2 p.7).
- Complexity O(k N^2) per pair; 155 s per pair of 1440-bin series on a laptop (p.9).
- Assumptions: direct calls only; transitive strength by chaining (p.10); asynchronous calls are a stated weakness (p.10).

## 4. Data and experimental setup
- TT: 25 services, 18 strong and 1 weak labels (Table II p.7). Industry: 192 services, 67 strong and 8 weak (Table II); only dependencies engineers knew were labelled (footnote p.7).
- Labels: two PhD students (TT) and senior engineers (Industry), consensus on disagreement.
- Parameters: bin 1 minute, round trip 0, drift 1 minute (Industry) or 0 (TT) (p.8). Bin sizes 1-10 minutes tested on Industry only.
- Leakage: none (unsupervised); but parameters are tuned on the evaluated data.

## 5. Results (copied)
| Metric | Theirs | Best baseline | Baseline name | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Industry CE / MAE / RMSE | 0.3270 / 0.1751 / 0.3044 | 0.6030 / 0.4501 / 0.4537 (best per column from Spearman) | correlation baselines | Table III p.8 |
| TT CE / MAE / RMSE | 0.4562 / 0.3435 / 0.3859 | 0.6464 (Kendall) / 0.3305 (Pearson) / 0.4388 (Pearson) | Pearson, Spearman, Kendall | Table III |
| DSW vs DTW on Industry | CE 0.3270 vs 0.3584 | n/a | AID_DTW | Table IV p.9 |
| Reduction on Industry | 45.8%, 61.1%, 33.2% (as stated) | n/a | n/a | p.9 |

- The 45.8% quoted for cross entropy matches 0.3270 vs 0.6030 (as reported). No statistical tests; one run.
- Case study: more than ten unnecessary dependencies found and optimised since deployment; engineer feedback only, no measured benefit (p.10).

## 6. Limitations
- Stated: labelling accuracy, small simulator with one weak dependency, asynchronous calls, indirect dependencies (pp.10).
- **My critique:**
  1. Task is dependency strength, not failure prediction; the "cascading failure prediction" framing is only motivation (p.2).
  2. Evaluation set is tiny and skewed: TT has 18 of 19 strong, so predicting "strong" everywhere scores well; Industry 67 of 75 strong (about 89%). A constant predictor of 0.89 would also be a natural baseline, not reported.
  3. Labels are binary and chosen by engineers for dependencies they knew; the continuous score is compared to 0/1.
  4. Baselines are correlation coefficients on the same series; no other dependency-mining methods (Rippler, CloudScout etc.) are run (p.11).
  5. Training-time and test-time parameters (drift, bin size) are set on the evaluation data.
  6. Stated "first": narrow claim (intensity from traces).
- Not discussed: label noise, confidence intervals, performance during an actual failure (the claimed cascading-failure use is anecdotal).

## 7. Reproducibility
- Code and data stated at github.com/OpsPAI/aid (not checked yet). Industrial data cannot be shared in full; the released set is described as released with the paper.

## 8. Comparison with OUR work
| Dimension | This paper | Ours (rca-lab) | Who is stronger, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Label requirement | none (labels for eval) | none | tie |
| Live / streaming | batch, anecdotal live use | incremental | ours (claimed) |
| Telemetry used | traces | traces (+ metrics) | similar |
| Propagation modelling | per-edge strength from time-warped similarity | learned edge probabilities | similar idea; theirs tested on edges |
| Forecasts future failures | no | claimed | n/a |
| Explanation | none | templates | ours |
| Evaluation rigor | 94 labelled edges, no CIs | synthetic | theirs has real data |
| Open / reproducible | stated | yes | tie |

- **What they have that we do not:** an evaluation of edge weights against engineer labels on a real cloud (Industry), and directed time-warping that handles caller-callee lag.
- **What we have that they do not:** use of the weights for RCA ranking and risk scoring; negative controls.
- **Could a reviewer say "this already exists"?** For "learn the strength of call edges from traces without labels": yes, partly. We must cite AID and compare our edge-weight estimator against its DSW similarity.
- **Position:** cite as prior work on label-free edge strength; do not call it failure prediction.
- **Must we run it as a baseline?** Yes, as a propagation-weight baseline if code is available.

## 9. Does this paper change what problem we should solve?
- It corrects my earlier reading of AID in `docs/REVIEW_REPORT.md` (it was described as predicting cascading impact; it estimates dependency strength). The gap "forecast cascade risk" is therefore less covered by AID than assumed, but "learn edge strength without labels" is covered.

## 10. Citation-ready facts (each with page)
- "AID derives a continuous dependency intensity from trace-derived invocation, error and duration series with a directed time-warping similarity" (pp.5-7).
- "On a Huawei Cloud region with 75 labelled dependencies, AID reached cross entropy 0.327 vs 0.603 for the best correlation baseline" (Table III p.8; note 67 of 75 labels are strong).

## 11. Open questions / things to verify
- Published venue; repo contents; whether AID's weights improve RCA ranking (not evaluated).

5	Dániel Unyi ,E r n˝oR i g ó , Bálint Gyires-Tóth , and Róbert Lovas
6	Abstract—Debugging cloud services is increasingly challeng-
7	ing due to their distributed, dynamic, and scalable nature.
8	Traditional methods struggle to handle large state spaces and the
9	complex interactions between microservices, making it difﬁcult
10	to diagnose failures and identify critical components. This paper
11	presents a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approach that
12	enhances cloud service debugging by predicting system-level fault
13	probabilities and providing interpretable insights into failure
14	propagation. Our method models microservice interactions as
15	graphs, where failures propagate probabilistically. Using Markov
16	Decision Processes (MDPs), we simulate failure behaviors,
17	capturing the probabilistic dependencies that inﬂuence system
18	reliability. The trained GNN not only predicts fault probabilities
19	but also identiﬁes the most failure-prone microservices and
20	explains their impact. We evaluate our approach on various ser-
21	vice mesh structures, including feature-enriched, tree-structured,
22	and general directed acyclic graph (DAG) architectures. Results
23	indicate that our method is effective in the operational phase
24	of cloud services, enabling proactive debugging and targeted
25	optimization. This work represents a step toward more inter-
26	pretable, reliable, and maintainable cloud infrastructures.

72	A. Cloud Computing With Reference Architecture and
73	Service Mesh Concepts
74	Cloud computing has transformed modern application
75	architectures by enabling scalable, on-demand resource pro-
76	visioning over the Internet. As cloud-native applications
77	continue to expand, microservices architectures [1] have
78	become the de facto standard for ensuring scalability, avail-
79	ability, and manageability. However, the heterogeneous and
80	distributed nature of microservices introduces challenges such
81	as efﬁcient orchestration, secure communication, and observ-
82	ability. Managing these interactions becomes particularly
83	difﬁcult as the number of microservices grows, increasing
84	the complexity of debugging and performance monitoring. To
85	address these issues, the service mesh paradigm has emerged
86	as a key solution.
87	A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that
88	manages service-to-service communication, ensuring transpar-
89	ent, reliable, and secure interactions between microservices.
90	It facilitates load balancing, service discovery, trafﬁc manage-
91	ment, failure recovery, and monitoring, signiﬁcantly reducing
92	the overhead associated with microservices orchestration. By
93	decoupling service communication from application logic, ser-
94	vice meshes simplify infrastructure management and enhance
95	observability. Complementing this, reference architectures [2],
96	[3], [4], [5], [6] serve as standardized blueprints for cloud
97	service design, incorporating best practices, interoperabil-
98	ity guidelines, and reliability principles to improve system
99	resilience.
100	Leading service mesh implementations–Istio, Linkerd, and
101	AWS App Mesh [7]–integrate reference architecture principles
102	to facilitate microservice communication and management.
103	For example, Istio provides advanced trafﬁc management,

120	B. Debugging Challenges
121	Debugging service mesh architectures can be challenging
122	due to their complexity and distributed nature [9]. A primary
123	issue is observability, which refers to analyzing system behav-
124	ior and inter-service communication. In practice, only partial
125	observability is often possible due to factors such as closed-
126	box (proprietary) services or probe effects, where monitoring
127	tools can inﬂuence system behavior. This incomplete view
128	makes it difﬁcult to determine which microservices contribute
129	most to system failures and how faults propagate through the
130	mesh.
131	Beyond observability, identifying and diagnosing faults
132	in large-scale service meshes is particularly challenging.
133	Conﬁguration errors, misrouted trafﬁc, and performance bot-
134	tlenecks can cause latency spikes, service degradation, and
135	system faults [10]. However, tracing these issues back to their
136	root cause is difﬁcult because service meshes abstract commu-
137	nication details, making failure propagation paths non-trivial
138	to reconstruct. Debugging inter-service failures is further
139	complicated by dynamic workloads and ephemeral service
140	instances, where failures may only manifest intermittently or
141	under speciﬁc operating conditions.
142	Additionally, failures in service meshes are often difﬁcult
143	to reproduce, making root cause analysis highly reactive
144	rather than proactive. Without effective replay mechanisms,
145	debugging relies on post-mortem analysis, where engineers
146	must manually analyze logs and traces, often with limited
147	visibility into how failures emerged. This lack of systematic
148	failure reproduction hinders efforts to anticipate and mitigate
149	faults before they escalate.

195	D. Proposed Debugging Framework
196	This paper shifts the focus from debugging during the
197	deployment phase to debugging during operation, where
198	failures often arise due to dynamic interactions between
199	microservices. Our approach introduces explainability into
200	debugging, using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to not only
201	predict system-level fault probabilities but also to provide
202	interpretable insights into failure propagation and root causes
203	(see black route in Figure 2). Unlike deterministic replay-
204	based debugging, which relies on replicating failure states, our
205	method uses observed data to improve fault localization and
206	guide debugging efforts.
207	Our approach builds on the service mesh paradigm, which
208	provides a structured, policy-driven environment for managing
209	microservices. Service mesh descriptors, such as those in Istio,
210	deﬁne critical conﬁgurations for network trafﬁc management
211	(e.g., routing rules, load balancing), security policies (e.g.,
212	authentication, authorization), and observability features (e.g.,
213	telemetry, logging). These descriptors allow ﬁne-grained con-
214	trol over service behavior without modifying application code,
215	making them an ideal foundation for our debugging framework
216	(Figure 2, “Service Mesh Description”).
217	The “ Predicate detection, active control, and debugging ”
218	approach is embedded within the “ Steering”-related compo-
219	nents of our framework (gray route in Figure 2). The ‘PRISM
220	simulator environment with model checker ’ detects suspicious
221	paths or nodes and labels them to steer debugging efforts
222	toward critical areas. In our previous work [12], we developed
223	a simpliﬁed service mesh model, representing RESTful service
224	nodes as a dependency tree. This was extended into a REST
225	modeling framework using a domain-speciﬁc language (DSL)
226	to deﬁne probabilistic service interactions, allowing the gen-
227	eration of probabilistic state machines for each microservice
228	based on its strategy and network connections. Our PRISM-
229	based model generator translates these DSL descriptions into
230	Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by generating module
231	descriptions in PRISM for all nodes and their dependencies.
232	Once validated, RESTful communication ﬂows of arbitrary
233	length can be simulated. Additionally, PRISM performs formal
234	veriﬁcation, ensuring the model satisﬁes speciﬁed correctness
235	properties using probabilistic model checking. This allows
236	us to deﬁne temporal logic properties and systematically
237	analyze failure cases, identifying deadlocks, inconsistencies,
238	and failure probabilities [13] (see ‘Generated & labeled traces’
239	in Fig. 2).

278	II. R ELATED WORKS
279	With the increasing complexity of cloud architec-
280	tures, maintaining system stability and fault detection has
281	become a critical challenge. Continuous monitoring collects
282	logs on memory issues, server failures, and application
283	performance [15], but the vast volume of logs makes it difﬁcult
284	to promptly isolate faults and take proactive measures before
285	system failures occur. Moreover, failure datasets are typically
286	much smaller than complete system logs, making fault analysis
287	challenging.
288	Farooq et al. deﬁne faults as abnormal conditions that
289	reduce or eliminate a component’s ability to function correctly,
290	with failures emerging as their observable consequences [16].
291	Identifying root causes before failures manifest is crucial for
292	proactive debugging.
293	Traditional formal veriﬁcation methods have been applied
294	to analyze cloud architectures, particularly in service-oriented
295	environments. Zatout et al. [17] propose transaction modeling
296	for improving reliability in RESTful applications, while
297	Souri et al. [18] review service composition veriﬁcation
298	techniques. These studies highlight the importance of formal
299	methods in ensuring the robustness of RESTful systems.
300	Although formal methods provide strong guarantees, their
301	applicability to large-scale, dynamic service meshes is limited
302	due to computational cost and reliance on predeﬁned models.
303	In order to address these limitations, data-driven fault detection
304	methods have emerged, using statistical analysis and machine
305	learning to improve fault diagnosis and prediction. The follow-
306	ing subsections discuss both traditional and ML-based fault
307	detection approaches, with a particular focus on GNN-based
308	methods for service meshes.
309	A. Traditional Fault Detection Methods
310	Rule-based fault detection methods, such as intrusion
311	and anomaly detection systems, monitor network or host
312	activity for deviations from expected behavior [19]. These
313	methods rely on either signature-based detection, using
314	predeﬁned anomaly patterns, or anomaly-based detection,
315	identifying statistical deviations from normal system behavior.
316	Abbasi et al. [20] propose an anomaly detection system for
317	cloud data centers that enhances fault resilience through real-
318	time monitoring and behavioral analysis.
319	Beyond anomaly detection, automated testing and
320	resilience strategies have been explored for service meshes.
321	Karn et al. [21] introduce a framework that monitors
322	microservice communication traces, using component
323	fault injectors to simulate delays, trafﬁc restrictions, and
324	terminations. Their approach detects faulty connections via
325	dashboards and mitigates issues through scaling, failover, and
326	circuit breakers, offering a reactive mechanism for service
327	reliability.
328	Formal modeling techniques have also been applied to
329	fault analysis in cloud environments. Cao and Niu [22] apply
330	higher-order Markov graphs to analyze cloud deployments and
331	big data logs, identifying complex failure patterns. However,
332	their approach lacks an active control mechanism to steer the
333	debugging process toward critical failure states.
334	Pontillo et al. [23] propose FERRARI, a failure reproduction
335	tool that generates test cases and analyzes stack traces to iden-
336	tify faults. FERRARI includes a similarity scoring mechanism
337	to estimate how closely generated test cases match real failure
338	conditions. While their tool aids in failure reproduction, it does
339	not incorporate ML-guided steering as in our work.
340	B. Machine Learning Based Fault Detection Methods
341	Machine learning-based fault detection methods generally
342	fall into supervised and unsupervised categories. Supervised
343	models learn to distinguish between normal and faulty behav-
344	ior using labeled input-output pairs, making them effective
345	when labeled data is available. In contrast, unsupervised
346	approaches detect anomalies by identifying deviations from
347	normal patterns without requiring explicit fault labels, allowing
348	them to adapt to previously unseen failure modes.
349	Zhang et al. [24] propose an online fault detection
350	model for cloud systems using a support vector machine
351	(SVM) with automated parameter tuning (SVM-Grid). Their
352	approach improves fault prediction by selecting relevant

395	C. Graph Neural Network Based Fault Detection
396	Maroudis et al. [28] investigate SLA violation prediction
397	using GNNs, exploring time series, content-based, and
398	context-based (graph-based) data representations. Their study
399	demonstrates that graph-based representations signiﬁcantly
400	enhance prediction accuracy by capturing the associativity of
401	clients and integrating them with traditional models. However,
402	their approach is concerned with SLA violations rather than
403	analyzing failure propagation or identifying structurally critical
404	components in cloud services.
405	Wu et al. [29] introduces MicroRCA, an attributed graph
406	model to trace anomaly propagation across services and
407	machines in microservice architectures. It performs real-time
408	root cause localization by correlating application performance
409	symptoms with system resource utilization. While effective for
410	diagnosing performance issues, its primary focus is on linking
411	performance anomalies to resource bottlenecks, making it
412	complementary to our work.
413	Wang et al. [30] applies hierarchical graph neural networks
414	to discover intra-network and cross-network causal depen-
415	dencies for fault localization. It combines topological causal
416	discovery with an Extreme Value Theory (EVT)-based method
417	to rank probable root causes. This approach is well-suited
418	for analyzing multi-level causal interactions but does not
419	explicitly account for the role of service dependencies in fault
420	propagation.
421	Gan et al. [31] introduce a trace-based root cause anal-
422	ysis system, Sleuth, for large-scale microservices, using an
423	unsupervised GNN to assess the causal impact of each span
424	in a trace. It clusters traces using a trace distance metric to
425	reduce the data volume required for root cause localization,
426	with a strong emphasis on transferability across microservice
427	applications. While Sleuth focuses on performance debugging,
428	our work provides a complementary perspective by learning
429	an explicit failure propagation model and identifying critical
430	subgraphs responsible for system faults.

467	III. M ODELLING SERVICE MESHES FOR CLOUD
468	REFERENCE ARCHITECTURES
469	A. Framework
470	Current modelling efforts build upon our previous work
471	focusing on probabilistic model checking applications, more
472	speciﬁcally the PRISM model checker [13] is employed to
473	describe, simulate and formally validate models expressed as
474	Markov decision processes (MDPs).
475	During further developments of the model, the PRISM
476	language is used to deﬁne parallel composition of modules
477	describing various behavioural patterns in different cloud
478	application modules. These patterns are composed of vari-
479	ous communication actions also serving as synchronization
480	points between the modules. Critical model parameters and
481	various features of interests are identiﬁed by PRISM labels
482	to aid tracking of behaviour changes in the cloud application.
483	Parametric generation of various experiments is based on
484	constants that provide a straightforward method to adjust
485	behavioural properties of the simulated application context.
486	Our work has gradually shifted from constrained or uncon-
487	strained path simulation applications towards formal model
488	checking against various properties described as probabilis-
489	tic linear temporal logical expressions, such as PCTL [33].
490	Ultimately, these expressions were used to deﬁne end-user
491	observable features of the simulated cloud application, most
492	prominently service availability or error rate provided by the
493	user interface.
494	B. Faults in a Cloud Application
495	Errors in a cloud application can result in either transient or
496	permanent disruption of their services. From the perspective of
497	end-users these disruptions result in performance degradation
498	or - in severe cases - functional or data losses.
499	Measurement efforts of cloud application quality aims to
500	quantify these properties. In cases of formal service agree-
501	ments, these quantitative metrics play a key role. Thresholds
502	for these metrics, including the acceptable rate of system
503	faults are often established in a Service Level Agreement
504	(SLA) between the cloud service provider and the end-user.
505	This kind of service measurement was ﬁrst employed in IP
506	networks [34]. The concept then was widely adopted by
507	various sectors, including cloud applications [35].
508	Although transient errors or permanent disruptions that
509	result in a performance degradation might play a major role
510	in overall debugging of a cloud application, for the time of
511	current research we are focusing on fatal service situations.
512	For this purpose service level is deﬁned as the probability of
513	fatal service disruption (system fault) observed by the end-
514	user. Contrary to the common practice of representing service
515	availability as the percentage ratio of acceptable metrics values
516	over time (e.g., requests are answered 99.995% within a
517	speciﬁc period of time), we are representing fatal system
518	disruption probability value (or in short, fault) as a standard
519	probability value (e.g., requests are failing with a probability
520	of 0.005 in the observed simulation window).
521	C. Service Mesh Architectures
522	In order to generalize and reﬁne our models further lever-
523	aging on our previous achievements [12], we continued to
524	investigate various methods of describing cloud use cases.
525	Microservice-based architecture patterns, also known as ser-
526	vice meshes, are becoming increasingly popular in modern
527	cloud applications [7].
528	Cloud applications were chosen to be modelled as a set
529	of loosely coupled Web services. Intra-application integration
530	is achieved by applying various services of the mesh service
531	component. From these integration services, message inter-
532	ception and routing is observed to be most feasible to aid in
533	simulation of RESTful cloud application services [36].
534	Our previous modelling efforts were aiming towards simpli-
535	ﬁed representation of a RESTful service model by organizing
536	application components by their dependency relationships
537	into a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where the root node
538	R is representing the user facing service component of the
539	application. In the model, R is continuously triggering requests
540	to intermediary nodes n and leaf nodes m. Requests are routed
541	in a nondeterministic way from R through various number of
542	intermediaries (n) ultimately arriving to a leaf m.
543	Two constants are introduced on the graph level to better
544	describe application behaviour Pfail is the probability of
545	failure of any leaf node ( m), while retries is a parameter
546	of intermediaries ( n) representing number of request re-
547	transmission attempts before giving up on an error. Responses
548	of the application are originating from leaf nodes ( m) then
549	propagated back through a series of intermediaries ( n)t ob e

668	A. Graph Neural Networks
669	Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the most
670	common machine learning methods for predictive tasks within
671	the domain of real-world networks. In these networks, each
672	individual data point corresponds to a node, characterized
673	not only by a feature vector xi but also an adjacency vector
674	ai that speciﬁes its connections to all other nodes. These
675	feature vectors are organized into a feature matrix denoted as

677	adjacency matrix A∈ RN×N , where F and N respectively
678	denote the number of features and the number of nodes in the

681	level, link-level, and graph-level tasks, depending on whether
682	the labels pertain to nodes, links, or entire graphs. Given the
683	sparsity of real-world networks, it is noteworthy that only a
684	small number of entries in A contain non-zero values. To
685	effectively handle such sparse matrices, GNNs incorporate
686	so-called message passing layers [37], [38]. Message-passing
687	layers are responsible for gathering information from neigh-
688	boring nodes. This process can be mathematically expressed
689	as:

709	B. GNN Training for Fault Prediction
710	To identify critical components within a service mesh,
711	it is essential to have a strong baseline GNN model for
712	fault probability prediction. With a well-trained model, we
713	can assess how the removal of certain parts of the service
714	mesh affects the system-level fault probability: a signiﬁcant
715	decrease indicates that those parts are weak components, while
716	a signiﬁcant increase suggests that those parts play a crucial
717	role in maintaining the service mesh’s performance.
718	Fault probability prediction is a graph-level regression task
719	in which each service mesh is represented as a graph, and the
720	target variable is the associated system-level fault probability.
721	Each node within the service mesh graph is characterized by
722	a single feature. For leaf nodes, this feature is the probability
723	of failure, while for intermediary nodes, it represents the
724	number of request retransmission attempts before giving up
725	on an error. To facilitate modeling, we employed two distinct
726	input channels: for leaves, the number of retries was set to
727	0 since they lack descendants, while for intermediaries, the
728	probability of failure was set to 0 as these nodes do not directly
729	experience failures. This approach ensures a consistent feature
730	representation.
731	The dataset was randomly split into training, validation,
732	and test sets, comprising 80%, 10%, and 10% of the service
733	meshes, respectively. Our objective is to learn a function f that
734	minimizes the mean squared error MSE (f (G), y) between the
735	predicted system-level fault probabilities f (G) and the ground-
736	truth system-level fault probabilities y for the input graphs
737	G =( X,A).
738	To achieve this, we use a standard graph neural network
739	architecture composed of the following layers: {MPBlock}→
740	{MPBlock}→{ MPBlock}→{ MPBlock}→
741	{GlobalMeanPool}→{ Linear}→{ ReLU}→{ Linear}
742	where each message passing block includes the follow-
743	ing operations: {MessagePassing}→{ BatchNorm}→
744	{PReLU}. The complete architecture is illustrated in
745	Figure 5.
746	We conducted meticulous hyperparameter tuning for our
747	GNN model. The dimensionality of each of the 4 hidden layers
748	were set to 32. The neural network was trained for 200 epochs
749	using mini-batches of 32 service meshes. Network parameters
750	were optimized using the Adam optimizer [39] with a learning
751	rate of 2e-4. The mean squared error (MSE) served as the loss
752	function. After training, we restored the parameters of the best
753	performing model on the validation set.
754	C. GNN Training for Identifying Critical Components
755	After developing a highly accurate GNN model for fault
756	prediction, we turned our attention to understanding how

760	speciﬁc parts of the service mesh inﬂuence the predicted
761	system-level fault probability. In each network, our goal is
762	to separate the network into two complementary parts: one
763	containing at most B% of the nodes and preserving prediction
764	accuracy (the relevant subgraph), and one where the prediction
765	accuracy degrades signiﬁcantly (the irrelevant subgraph). This
766	way, the selected nodes are both necessary and sufﬁcient for
767	the prediction. Exhaustively searching for such subnetworks
768	by evaluating all possible node subsets is computationally
769	infeasible, which motivates the need for a learned masking
770	mechanism.
771	To address this challenge, we designed an explainability
772	algorithm that assigns importance scores to the nodes of
773	a network. Drawing inspiration from previous methods like
774	L2X [40], INV ASE[41], and PGExplainer [42], our approach
775	uses an explainer neural network to compute node importance
776	probabilities via gradient descent. Based on these probabilities,
777	we can select the most important B% of the nodes in the
778	service mesh with respect to fault prediction, providing a
779	practical solution to our problem that minimizes prediction
780	error.
781	Our algorithm, depicted in Figure 6, consists of two neural
782	networks: an explainer GNN and a predictor GNN. The
783	explainer GNN generates a Bernoulli distribution over the
784	nodes of the service mesh, as illustrated in Figure 7.T h e
785	probabilities assigned to each node reﬂect its signiﬁcance in
786	shaping the fault prediction process. From this distribution,
787	we can sample a node mask that selects the most important
788	nodes. This mask is then applied to both the adjacency
789	matrix A and the feature matrix X through element-wise
790	multiplication, producing a masked version of the input graph.
791	The predictor GNN, trained for fault prediction as described
792	in the previous subsection, evaluates three versions of the
793	graph: the original unmasked graph G, the subgraph selected
794	by the explainer after masking g, and its complementary
795	subgraph ¯g (the nodes not selected by the explainer). If
796	the node mask captures the most relevant nodes within the
797	service mesh, the predictor’s performance on the selected
798	subgraph g should closely approximate its performance on the
799	original graph G, while its performance on the complementary
800	subgraph ¯g should drop signiﬁcantly. This demonstrates that
801	the selected nodes are really the critical components driving
802	the fault prediction: they are necessary because removing them
803	signiﬁcantly impacts the prediction, and sufﬁcient because the
804	subgraph alone can replicate the original prediction.
805	The explainer and predictor GNNs are trained in alternating
806	steps. In each iteration:
807	• Predictor update: The explainer generates a probability
808	distribution p over the nodes of the graph. A node mask
809	m is then sampled by applying Bernoulli sampling to
810	this probability distribution. This mask deﬁnes a selected
811	subgraph g and its complementary subgraph ¯g.T h e
812	predictor f is trained to minimize the mean squared error
813	(MSE) between its predictions and the true system-level
814	fault probability on both subgraphs:
815	Lf = MSE(f (g), y)+ MSE(f (¯g), y)
816	• Explainer update: The predictor, with its updated param-
817	eters, is evaluated on the subgraphs g and ¯g to compute
818	the reward. The explainer s is then optimized using the
819	REINFORCE algorithm [43] with the loss:
820	Ls = R · BCE(p, m)
821	where the reward function R is based on the difference
822	between the predictor’s performance on the selected
823	subgraph and its complementary subgraph, with an added
824	term that encourages sparsity in the selected nodes [42]:
825	R = MSE(f (¯g), y) − MSE(f (g), y)+ ReLU

827	μp − B
828	)
829	Here, μp is the mean of the probability distribution p,
830	and B is the budget which controls the expected number
831	of nodes selected by the explainer.
832	The dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets
833	following the same procedure used for fault prediction, and
834	the same hyperparameters were retained.
835	D. Computational Complexity
836	Our approach is computationally efﬁcient, as both the fault
837	probability estimation and the explainability algorithm rely
838	on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The key property of
839	GNNs is that they operate on sparse adjacency matrices,
840	enabling efﬁcient storage and computation. The computational
841	complexity of message-passing layers in GNNs is O(E),
842	where E is the number of edges in the graph. Since service
843	meshes typically have far fewer edges than the theoretical
844	O(N2) bound for dense graphs, this makes GNN-based fault
845	probability estimation scalable even for large-scale systems.
846	Since our explainer network is implemented as another
847	GNN that learns to generate node importance scores, its
848	complexity remains the same as the fault probability predictor
849	GNN. Its overhead comes from sampling node masks and
850	computing the reward function, but these operations are
851	lightweight compared to the forward and backward passes of
852	a GNN.

856	masking, producing a mask that selects the most important nodes for fault probability prediction. The predictor GNN then evaluates the selected subg raph g
857	and its complementary ¯g. If the mask captures the most relevant nodes, the predictor’s performance on the subgraph g should closely match its performance
858	on the original graph, while its performance on the complementary subgraph ¯g should drop signiﬁcantly, conﬁrming that the selected nodes are necessary
859	and sufﬁcient for the prediction. The mean of the probabilities, µp , and the budget B (e.g., B = 33% means one-third of the nodes are retained) control the
860	number of nodes selected.
861	Fig. 7. The explainer network consists of six message-passing blocks,

863	nodes, reﬂecting their importance for fault probability prediction.
864	V. E XPERIMENT 1: FAULT PREDICTION FOR FEATURE
865	ENRICHED SERVICE MESHES
866	In this experiment, we evaluate the performance of our
867	GNN-based approach for fault prediction on two types of ser-
868	vice meshes: tree-shaped service meshes and general directed
869	acyclic graphs (DAGs). Fault prediction serves as a foundation
870	for identifying critical components within the service mesh,
871	as accurately predicting system fault probabilities allows us to
872	analyze the impact of removing speciﬁc nodes. Tree-shaped
873	meshes represent a simpler hierarchical topology, making it
874	easier to trace service dependencies, whereas general DAGs
875	capture more complex, non-hierarchical relationships between
876	services, where identifying critical components might be more
877	challenging. All experiments were repeated three times, and
878	all results reported are the mean and standard deviation across
879	these three runs.
880	A. Training Dataset
881	The generation of training datasets for the REST-based
882	approach involves constructing synthetic models that simulate
883	complex cloud architectures characterized by a service mesh
884	pattern. The RESTful services are designed as nodes within a
885	directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure, where the root node
886	initiates requests that propagate through intermediary nodes
887	to leaf nodes. Intermediary nodes handle requests probabilis-
888	tically, relaying them towards child nodes or providing direct
889	responses. Leaf nodes ﬁnalize interactions by returning HTTP
890	status codes, either signifying successful operations (HTTP
891	2xx) or indicating server failures (HTTP 5xx), the latter of
892	which triggers a deﬁned retry mechanism. Each component’s
893	operations and interactions are probabilistically modulated,
894	enabling varied simulations reﬂective of real-world scenarios.
895	Utilizing the Python programming language, a domain-speciﬁc
896	language (DSL) was devised to model these interactions
897	within the RESTful framework. This automation facilitates
898	the creation and execution of extensive simulations, with
899	predeﬁned ranges for critical parameters such as the number of
900	items and buffer sizes, enhancing the robustness of the dataset.

Explainable GNN-Based Approach to Fault
Forecasting in Cloud Service Debugging
Dániel Unyi ,E r n˝oR i g ó , Bálint Gyires-Tóth , and Róbert Lovas
Abstract—Debugging cloud services is increasingly challeng-
ing due to their distributed, dynamic, and scalable nature.
Traditional methods struggle to handle large state spaces and the
complex interactions between microservices, making it difﬁcult
to diagnose failures and identify critical components. This paper
presents a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approach that
enhances cloud service debugging by predicting system-level fault
probabilities and providing interpretable insights into failure
propagation. Our method models microservice interactions as
graphs, where failures propagate probabilistically. Using Markov
Decision Processes (MDPs), we simulate failure behaviors,
capturing the probabilistic dependencies that inﬂuence system
reliability. The trained GNN not only predicts fault probabilities
but also identiﬁes the most failure-prone microservices and
explains their impact. We evaluate our approach on various ser-
vice mesh structures, including feature-enriched, tree-structured,
and general directed acyclic graph (DAG) architectures. Results
indicate that our method is effective in the operational phase
of cloud services, enabling proactive debugging and targeted
optimization. This work represents a step toward more inter-
pretable, reliable, and maintainable cloud infrastructures.
Index Terms—Cloud computing, software debugging, microser-
vice architectures, deep learning, graph neural networks,
explainable AI, fault prediction.
I. I NTRODUCTION
C
LOUD computing’s distributed, dynamic, and scalable
nature makes debugging cloud services increasingly
complex. Traditional debugging, monitoring, and troubleshoot-
ing methods struggle to capture the dependencies between

microservices. One of the greatest challenges in debugging is
not just detecting failures, but understanding why they occur
and which components are responsible. Debugging tools must
move beyond simple anomaly detection and provide inter-
pretable insights that highlight the root causes of failures and
the most inﬂuential microservices affecting system reliability.
To ensure high availability and reliability, there is a critical
need for explainable methods that analyze, predict, and clarify
cloud service behavior. To bridge this gap, our work integrates
failure propagation modeling with GNN-based explainability,
which allows both fault probability estimation and critical
component identiﬁcation within service meshes.
A. Cloud Computing With Reference Architecture and
Service Mesh Concepts
Cloud computing has transformed modern application
architectures by enabling scalable, on-demand resource pro-
visioning over the Internet. As cloud-native applications
continue to expand, microservices architectures [1] have
become the de facto standard for ensuring scalability, avail-
ability, and manageability. However, the heterogeneous and
distributed nature of microservices introduces challenges such
as efﬁcient orchestration, secure communication, and observ-
ability. Managing these interactions becomes particularly
difﬁcult as the number of microservices grows, increasing
the complexity of debugging and performance monitoring. To
address these issues, the service mesh paradigm has emerged
as a key solution.
A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that
manages service-to-service communication, ensuring transpar-
ent, reliable, and secure interactions between microservices.
It facilitates load balancing, service discovery, trafﬁc manage-
ment, failure recovery, and monitoring, signiﬁcantly reducing
the overhead associated with microservices orchestration. By
decoupling service communication from application logic, ser-
vice meshes simplify infrastructure management and enhance
observability. Complementing this, reference architectures [2],
[3], [4], [5], [6] serve as standardized blueprints for cloud
service design, incorporating best practices, interoperabil-
ity guidelines, and reliability principles to improve system
resilience.
Leading service mesh implementations–Istio, Linkerd, and
AWS App Mesh [7]–integrate reference architecture principles
to facilitate microservice communication and management.
For example, Istio provides advanced trafﬁc management,
security policies, and telemetry collection, establishing a

UNYI et al.: EXPLAINABLE GNN-BASED APPROACH TO FAULT FORECASTING 5641
Fig. 1. Classiﬁcation of general distributed debugging methodologies [8] extended with our planned results in service mesh environment (grey background).
strong foundation for operational control and observability.
However, while these tools enhance visibility into service
interactions, analyzing failure propagation across microser-
vices remains a challenge, requiring additional techniques to
assess system reliability and performance.
In summary, service meshes and reference architectures
improve operational efﬁciency, security, and observability,
but effectively analyzing service behavior still requires addi-
tional tools that can track dependencies and evaluate system
performance under failure conditions.
B. Debugging Challenges
Debugging service mesh architectures can be challenging
due to their complexity and distributed nature [9]. A primary
issue is observability, which refers to analyzing system behav-
ior and inter-service communication. In practice, only partial
observability is often possible due to factors such as closed-
box (proprietary) services or probe effects, where monitoring
tools can inﬂuence system behavior. This incomplete view
makes it difﬁcult to determine which microservices contribute
most to system failures and how faults propagate through the
mesh.
Beyond observability, identifying and diagnosing faults
in large-scale service meshes is particularly challenging.
Conﬁguration errors, misrouted trafﬁc, and performance bot-
tlenecks can cause latency spikes, service degradation, and
system faults [10]. However, tracing these issues back to their
root cause is difﬁcult because service meshes abstract commu-
nication details, making failure propagation paths non-trivial
to reconstruct. Debugging inter-service failures is further
complicated by dynamic workloads and ephemeral service
instances, where failures may only manifest intermittently or
under speciﬁc operating conditions.
Additionally, failures in service meshes are often difﬁcult
to reproduce, making root cause analysis highly reactive
rather than proactive. Without effective replay mechanisms,
debugging relies on post-mortem analysis, where engineers
must manually analyze logs and traces, often with limited
visibility into how failures emerged. This lack of systematic
failure reproduction hinders efforts to anticipate and mitigate
faults before they escalate.
C. Theoretical Background and Research Plan
Distributed debugging methodologies can be classiﬁed
based on their support for global predicate speciﬁcation and
detection, as well as their ability to identify root causes of
software bugs in distributed systems [8]. Over time, these
methodologies have evolved to address the limitations of
previous approaches. Figure 1 summarizes these methods and
highlights our planned contributions in service mesh environ-
ments (grey background).
At the most basic level, interactive debugging extends
traditional sequential debugging to remote processes, allowing
real-time monitoring but lacking insight into inter-process
interactions, making it unsuitable for distributed systems. To
overcome this, the “ Trace, replay and debugging ” approach
(Figure 1, row 2) records selected execution traces to enable
deterministic reproduction of faulty behaviors under controlled
conditions.
Building on this, the “ Integrated testing, active control
and debugging” (Figure 1, row 3) introduces mechanisms that
steer execution along predeﬁned computation paths, improving
=== page 3 ===
5642 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT, VOL. 22, NO. 6, DECEMBER 2025
Fig. 2. Proposed framework for debugging cycle with tools and dataﬂow.
reproducibility beyond passive observation. A more advanced
technique, “Predicate detection, active control and debugging”
(Figure 1, row 4), allows users to deﬁne correctness conditions
(predicates) that are continuously evaluated during execution,
enhancing systematic failure detection.
One of our previous works extended this methodology to
the deployment phase of orchestrated cloud services [11],
focusing on improving reliability (including platform-agnostic
behavior) in complex deployment strategies. This approach
proved useful in detecting timing or architecture-dependent
failures within deployment descriptions and orchestration
steps.
This research further narrows the scope to developing
a smart steering mechanism within the “Smart Control,
Debugging, and Evaluation” paradigm (Figure 1,r o w5 ) .I n
our previous work [12], we applied the PRISM simulator envi-

Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and Graph Neural

beyond this, in this paper we focus on leveraging GNNs for
fault prediction and explainability to enhance debugging in
cloud service meshes.
D. Proposed Debugging Framework
This paper shifts the focus from debugging during the
deployment phase to debugging during operation, where
failures often arise due to dynamic interactions between
microservices. Our approach introduces explainability into
debugging, using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to not only
predict system-level fault probabilities but also to provide
interpretable insights into failure propagation and root causes
(see black route in Figure 2). Unlike deterministic replay-
based debugging, which relies on replicating failure states, our
method uses observed data to improve fault localization and
guide debugging efforts.
Our approach builds on the service mesh paradigm, which
provides a structured, policy-driven environment for managing
microservices. Service mesh descriptors, such as those in Istio,
deﬁne critical conﬁgurations for network trafﬁc management
(e.g., routing rules, load balancing), security policies (e.g.,
authentication, authorization), and observability features (e.g.,
telemetry, logging). These descriptors allow ﬁne-grained con-
trol over service behavior without modifying application code,
making them an ideal foundation for our debugging framework
(Figure 2, “Service Mesh Description”).
The “ Predicate detection, active control, and debugging ”
approach is embedded within the “ Steering”-related compo-
nents of our framework (gray route in Figure 2). The ‘PRISM
simulator environment with model checker ’ detects suspicious
paths or nodes and labels them to steer debugging efforts
toward critical areas. In our previous work [12], we developed
a simpliﬁed service mesh model, representing RESTful service
nodes as a dependency tree. This was extended into a REST
modeling framework using a domain-speciﬁc language (DSL)
to deﬁne probabilistic service interactions, allowing the gen-
eration of probabilistic state machines for each microservice
based on its strategy and network connections. Our PRISM-
based model generator translates these DSL descriptions into
Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by generating module
descriptions in PRISM for all nodes and their dependencies.
Once validated, RESTful communication ﬂows of arbitrary
length can be simulated. Additionally, PRISM performs formal
veriﬁcation, ensuring the model satisﬁes speciﬁed correctness
properties using probabilistic model checking. This allows
us to deﬁne temporal logic properties and systematically
analyze failure cases, identifying deadlocks, inconsistencies,
and failure probabilities [13] (see ‘Generated & labeled traces’
in Fig. 2).

II. R ELATED WORKS
With the increasing complexity of cloud architec-
tures, maintaining system stability and fault detection has
become a critical challenge. Continuous monitoring collects
logs on memory issues, server failures, and application
performance [15], but the vast volume of logs makes it difﬁcult
to promptly isolate faults and take proactive measures before
system failures occur. Moreover, failure datasets are typically
much smaller than complete system logs, making fault analysis
challenging.
Farooq et al. deﬁne faults as abnormal conditions that
reduce or eliminate a component’s ability to function correctly,
with failures emerging as their observable consequences [16].
Identifying root causes before failures manifest is crucial for
proactive debugging.
Traditional formal veriﬁcation methods have been applied
to analyze cloud architectures, particularly in service-oriented
environments. Zatout et al. [17] propose transaction modeling
for improving reliability in RESTful applications, while
Souri et al. [18] review service composition veriﬁcation
techniques. These studies highlight the importance of formal
methods in ensuring the robustness of RESTful systems.
Although formal methods provide strong guarantees, their
applicability to large-scale, dynamic service meshes is limited
due to computational cost and reliance on predeﬁned models.
In order to address these limitations, data-driven fault detection
methods have emerged, using statistical analysis and machine
learning to improve fault diagnosis and prediction. The follow-
ing subsections discuss both traditional and ML-based fault
detection approaches, with a particular focus on GNN-based
methods for service meshes.
A. Traditional Fault Detection Methods
Rule-based fault detection methods, such as intrusion
and anomaly detection systems, monitor network or host
activity for deviations from expected behavior [19]. These
methods rely on either signature-based detection, using
predeﬁned anomaly patterns, or anomaly-based detection,
identifying statistical deviations from normal system behavior.
Abbasi et al. [20] propose an anomaly detection system for
cloud data centers that enhances fault resilience through real-
time monitoring and behavioral analysis.
Beyond anomaly detection, automated testing and
resilience strategies have been explored for service meshes.
Karn et al. [21] introduce a framework that monitors
microservice communication traces, using component
fault injectors to simulate delays, trafﬁc restrictions, and
terminations. Their approach detects faulty connections via
dashboards and mitigates issues through scaling, failover, and
circuit breakers, offering a reactive mechanism for service
reliability.
Formal modeling techniques have also been applied to
fault analysis in cloud environments. Cao and Niu [22] apply
higher-order Markov graphs to analyze cloud deployments and
big data logs, identifying complex failure patterns. However,
their approach lacks an active control mechanism to steer the
debugging process toward critical failure states.
Pontillo et al. [23] propose FERRARI, a failure reproduction
tool that generates test cases and analyzes stack traces to iden-
tify faults. FERRARI includes a similarity scoring mechanism
to estimate how closely generated test cases match real failure
conditions. While their tool aids in failure reproduction, it does
not incorporate ML-guided steering as in our work.
B. Machine Learning Based Fault Detection Methods
Machine learning-based fault detection methods generally
fall into supervised and unsupervised categories. Supervised
models learn to distinguish between normal and faulty behav-
ior using labeled input-output pairs, making them effective
when labeled data is available. In contrast, unsupervised
approaches detect anomalies by identifying deviations from
normal patterns without requiring explicit fault labels, allowing
them to adapt to previously unseen failure modes.
Zhang et al. [24] propose an online fault detection
model for cloud systems using a support vector machine
(SVM) with automated parameter tuning (SVM-Grid). Their
approach improves fault prediction by selecting relevant

Zhou et al. [25] introduce MEPFL, a machine learning-
based method for latent error prediction and fault localization
in microservice applications. It leverages system trace logs to
train models at both the trace and microservice levels, allowing
real-time fault detection and classiﬁcation. By analyzing exe-

MEPFL improves failure diagnosis in dynamic production
environments. However, it primarily focuses on predicting
fault occurrences rather than modeling how failures propagate
within a service mesh.
Meng et al. [26] present a reinforcement learning approach
to predict fault resilience behaviors in service meshes.
Their method optimizes service-level conﬁgurations that
inﬂuence request-response behavior under failure conditions,
which enables adaptive fault resilience strategies across both
individual services and multi-service orchestrations. While
effective for mitigating faults, this approach emphasizes pol-
icy optimization rather than failure probability estimation or
interpretable fault propagation modeling.
Rouf et al. [27] propose InstantOps, a multi-modal failure
prediction and root cause analysis (RCA) framework that
integrates logs, metrics, traces, and microservices events. It
constructs a dynamic service call ﬂow graph, where traces
deﬁne the structure, while logs and resource metrics enrich
node attributes. InstantOps applies GNNs to capture spatial
dependencies and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) to model
temporal failure patterns, enabling proactive failure prediction
and precise root cause localization. Moreover, permutation
testing is used to assess node importance within failure propa-
gation chains. While InstantOps effectively fuses multi-modal
observability data and models both spatial and temporal failure
dynamics, it differs from our work, which explicitly learns
a failure propagation model to identify critical subgraphs
contributing to system faults.
C. Graph Neural Network Based Fault Detection
Maroudis et al. [28] investigate SLA violation prediction
using GNNs, exploring time series, content-based, and
context-based (graph-based) data representations. Their study
demonstrates that graph-based representations signiﬁcantly
enhance prediction accuracy by capturing the associativity of
clients and integrating them with traditional models. However,
their approach is concerned with SLA violations rather than
analyzing failure propagation or identifying structurally critical
components in cloud services.
Wu et al. [29] introduces MicroRCA, an attributed graph
model to trace anomaly propagation across services and
machines in microservice architectures. It performs real-time
root cause localization by correlating application performance
symptoms with system resource utilization. While effective for
diagnosing performance issues, its primary focus is on linking
performance anomalies to resource bottlenecks, making it
complementary to our work.
Wang et al. [30] applies hierarchical graph neural networks
to discover intra-network and cross-network causal depen-
dencies for fault localization. It combines topological causal
discovery with an Extreme Value Theory (EVT)-based method
to rank probable root causes. This approach is well-suited
for analyzing multi-level causal interactions but does not
explicitly account for the role of service dependencies in fault
propagation.
Gan et al. [31] introduce a trace-based root cause anal-
ysis system, Sleuth, for large-scale microservices, using an
unsupervised GNN to assess the causal impact of each span
in a trace. It clusters traces using a trace distance metric to
reduce the data volume required for root cause localization,
with a strong emphasis on transferability across microservice
applications. While Sleuth focuses on performance debugging,
our work provides a complementary perspective by learning
an explicit failure propagation model and identifying critical
subgraphs responsible for system faults.

III. M ODELLING SERVICE MESHES FOR CLOUD
REFERENCE ARCHITECTURES
A. Framework
Current modelling efforts build upon our previous work
focusing on probabilistic model checking applications, more
speciﬁcally the PRISM model checker [13] is employed to
describe, simulate and formally validate models expressed as
Markov decision processes (MDPs).
During further developments of the model, the PRISM
language is used to deﬁne parallel composition of modules
describing various behavioural patterns in different cloud
application modules. These patterns are composed of vari-
ous communication actions also serving as synchronization
points between the modules. Critical model parameters and
various features of interests are identiﬁed by PRISM labels
to aid tracking of behaviour changes in the cloud application.
Parametric generation of various experiments is based on
constants that provide a straightforward method to adjust
behavioural properties of the simulated application context.
Our work has gradually shifted from constrained or uncon-
strained path simulation applications towards formal model
checking against various properties described as probabilis-
tic linear temporal logical expressions, such as PCTL [33].
Ultimately, these expressions were used to deﬁne end-user
observable features of the simulated cloud application, most
prominently service availability or error rate provided by the
user interface.
B. Faults in a Cloud Application
Errors in a cloud application can result in either transient or
permanent disruption of their services. From the perspective of
end-users these disruptions result in performance degradation
or - in severe cases - functional or data losses.
Measurement efforts of cloud application quality aims to
quantify these properties. In cases of formal service agree-
ments, these quantitative metrics play a key role. Thresholds
for these metrics, including the acceptable rate of system
faults are often established in a Service Level Agreement
(SLA) between the cloud service provider and the end-user.
This kind of service measurement was ﬁrst employed in IP
networks [34]. The concept then was widely adopted by
various sectors, including cloud applications [35].
Although transient errors or permanent disruptions that
result in a performance degradation might play a major role
in overall debugging of a cloud application, for the time of
current research we are focusing on fatal service situations.
For this purpose service level is deﬁned as the probability of
fatal service disruption (system fault) observed by the end-
user. Contrary to the common practice of representing service
availability as the percentage ratio of acceptable metrics values
over time (e.g., requests are answered 99.995% within a
speciﬁc period of time), we are representing fatal system
disruption probability value (or in short, fault) as a standard
probability value (e.g., requests are failing with a probability
of 0.005 in the observed simulation window).
C. Service Mesh Architectures
In order to generalize and reﬁne our models further lever-
aging on our previous achievements [12], we continued to
investigate various methods of describing cloud use cases.
Microservice-based architecture patterns, also known as ser-
vice meshes, are becoming increasingly popular in modern
cloud applications [7].
Cloud applications were chosen to be modelled as a set
of loosely coupled Web services. Intra-application integration
is achieved by applying various services of the mesh service
component. From these integration services, message inter-
ception and routing is observed to be most feasible to aid in
simulation of RESTful cloud application services [36].
Our previous modelling efforts were aiming towards simpli-
ﬁed representation of a RESTful service model by organizing
application components by their dependency relationships
into a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where the root node
R is representing the user facing service component of the
application. In the model, R is continuously triggering requests
to intermediary nodes n and leaf nodes m. Requests are routed
in a nondeterministic way from R through various number of
intermediaries (n) ultimately arriving to a leaf m.
Two constants are introduced on the graph level to better
describe application behaviour Pfail is the probability of
failure of any leaf node ( m), while retries is a parameter
of intermediaries ( n) representing number of request re-
transmission attempts before giving up on an error. Responses
of the application are originating from leaf nodes ( m) then
propagated back through a series of intermediaries ( n)t ob e
ultimately aggregated at R enabling observation of application
error rates.

IV . GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK FOR THE DETECTION OF
CRITICAL COMPONENTS IN SERVICE MESHES
A. Graph Neural Networks
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the most
common machine learning methods for predictive tasks within
the domain of real-world networks. In these networks, each
individual data point corresponds to a node, characterized
not only by a feature vector xi but also an adjacency vector
ai that speciﬁes its connections to all other nodes. These
feature vectors are organized into a feature matrix denoted as
X∈ RN×F , while the adjacency vectors take the form of an
adjacency matrix A∈ RN×N , where F and N respectively
denote the number of features and the number of nodes in the
network.
The tasks addressed by GNNs can be categorized into node-
level, link-level, and graph-level tasks, depending on whether
the labels pertain to nodes, links, or entire graphs. Given the
sparsity of real-world networks, it is noteworthy that only a
small number of entries in A contain non-zero values. To
effectively handle such sparse matrices, GNNs incorporate
so-called message passing layers [37], [38]. Message-passing
layers are responsible for gathering information from neigh-
boring nodes. This process can be mathematically expressed
as:

B. GNN Training for Fault Prediction
To identify critical components within a service mesh,
it is essential to have a strong baseline GNN model for
fault probability prediction. With a well-trained model, we
can assess how the removal of certain parts of the service
mesh affects the system-level fault probability: a signiﬁcant
decrease indicates that those parts are weak components, while
a signiﬁcant increase suggests that those parts play a crucial
role in maintaining the service mesh’s performance.
Fault probability prediction is a graph-level regression task
in which each service mesh is represented as a graph, and the
target variable is the associated system-level fault probability.
Each node within the service mesh graph is characterized by
a single feature. For leaf nodes, this feature is the probability
of failure, while for intermediary nodes, it represents the
number of request retransmission attempts before giving up
on an error. To facilitate modeling, we employed two distinct
input channels: for leaves, the number of retries was set to
0 since they lack descendants, while for intermediaries, the
probability of failure was set to 0 as these nodes do not directly
experience failures. This approach ensures a consistent feature
representation.
The dataset was randomly split into training, validation,
and test sets, comprising 80%, 10%, and 10% of the service
meshes, respectively. Our objective is to learn a function f that
minimizes the mean squared error MSE (f (G), y) between the
predicted system-level fault probabilities f (G) and the ground-
truth system-level fault probabilities y for the input graphs
G =( X,A).
To achieve this, we use a standard graph neural network
architecture composed of the following layers: {MPBlock}→
{MPBlock}→{ MPBlock}→{ MPBlock}→
{GlobalMeanPool}→{ Linear}→{ ReLU}→{ Linear}
where each message passing block includes the follow-
ing operations: {MessagePassing}→{ BatchNorm}→
{PReLU}. The complete architecture is illustrated in
Figure 5.
We conducted meticulous hyperparameter tuning for our
GNN model. The dimensionality of each of the 4 hidden layers
were set to 32. The neural network was trained for 200 epochs
using mini-batches of 32 service meshes. Network parameters
were optimized using the Adam optimizer [39] with a learning
rate of 2e-4. The mean squared error (MSE) served as the loss
function. After training, we restored the parameters of the best
performing model on the validation set.
C. GNN Training for Identifying Critical Components
After developing a highly accurate GNN model for fault
prediction, we turned our attention to understanding how

speciﬁc parts of the service mesh inﬂuence the predicted
system-level fault probability. In each network, our goal is
to separate the network into two complementary parts: one
containing at most B% of the nodes and preserving prediction
accuracy (the relevant subgraph), and one where the prediction
accuracy degrades signiﬁcantly (the irrelevant subgraph). This
way, the selected nodes are both necessary and sufﬁcient for
the prediction. Exhaustively searching for such subnetworks
by evaluating all possible node subsets is computationally
infeasible, which motivates the need for a learned masking
mechanism.
To address this challenge, we designed an explainability
algorithm that assigns importance scores to the nodes of
a network. Drawing inspiration from previous methods like
L2X [40], INV ASE[41], and PGExplainer [42], our approach
uses an explainer neural network to compute node importance
probabilities via gradient descent. Based on these probabilities,
we can select the most important B% of the nodes in the
service mesh with respect to fault prediction, providing a
practical solution to our problem that minimizes prediction
error.
Our algorithm, depicted in Figure 6, consists of two neural
networks: an explainer GNN and a predictor GNN. The
explainer GNN generates a Bernoulli distribution over the
nodes of the service mesh, as illustrated in Figure 7.T h e
probabilities assigned to each node reﬂect its signiﬁcance in
shaping the fault prediction process. From this distribution,
we can sample a node mask that selects the most important
nodes. This mask is then applied to both the adjacency
matrix A and the feature matrix X through element-wise
multiplication, producing a masked version of the input graph.
The predictor GNN, trained for fault prediction as described
in the previous subsection, evaluates three versions of the
graph: the original unmasked graph G, the subgraph selected
by the explainer after masking g, and its complementary
subgraph ¯g (the nodes not selected by the explainer). If
the node mask captures the most relevant nodes within the
service mesh, the predictor’s performance on the selected
subgraph g should closely approximate its performance on the
original graph G, while its performance on the complementary
subgraph ¯g should drop signiﬁcantly. This demonstrates that
the selected nodes are really the critical components driving
the fault prediction: they are necessary because removing them
signiﬁcantly impacts the prediction, and sufﬁcient because the
subgraph alone can replicate the original prediction.
The explainer and predictor GNNs are trained in alternating
steps. In each iteration:
• Predictor update: The explainer generates a probability
distribution p over the nodes of the graph. A node mask
m is then sampled by applying Bernoulli sampling to

D. Computational Complexity
Our approach is computationally efﬁcient, as both the fault
probability estimation and the explainability algorithm rely
on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The key property of
GNNs is that they operate on sparse adjacency matrices,
enabling efﬁcient storage and computation. The computational
complexity of message-passing layers in GNNs is O(E),
where E is the number of edges in the graph. Since service
meshes typically have far fewer edges than the theoretical
O(N2) bound for dense graphs, this makes GNN-based fault
probability estimation scalable even for large-scale systems.
Since our explainer network is implemented as another
GNN that learns to generate node importance scores, its
complexity remains the same as the fault probability predictor
GNN. Its overhead comes from sampling node masks and
computing the reward function, but these operations are
lightweight compared to the forward and backward passes of
a GNN.

V. E XPERIMENT 1: FAULT PREDICTION FOR FEATURE
ENRICHED SERVICE MESHES
In this experiment, we evaluate the performance of our
GNN-based approach for fault prediction on two types of ser-
vice meshes: tree-shaped service meshes and general directed
acyclic graphs (DAGs). Fault prediction serves as a foundation
for identifying critical components within the service mesh,
as accurately predicting system fault probabilities allows us to
analyze the impact of removing speciﬁc nodes. Tree-shaped
meshes represent a simpler hierarchical topology, making it
easier to trace service dependencies, whereas general DAGs
capture more complex, non-hierarchical relationships between
services, where identifying critical components might be more
challenging. All experiments were repeated three times, and
all results reported are the mean and standard deviation across
these three runs.
A. Training Dataset
The generation of training datasets for the REST-based
approach involves constructing synthetic models that simulate
complex cloud architectures characterized by a service mesh
pattern. The RESTful services are designed as nodes within a
directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure, where the root node
initiates requests that propagate through intermediary nodes
to leaf nodes. Intermediary nodes handle requests probabilis-
tically, relaying them towards child nodes or providing direct
responses. Leaf nodes ﬁnalize interactions by returning HTTP
status codes, either signifying successful operations (HTTP
2xx) or indicating server failures (HTTP 5xx), the latter of
which triggers a deﬁned retry mechanism. Each component’s
operations and interactions are probabilistically modulated,
enabling varied simulations reﬂective of real-world scenarios.
Utilizing the Python programming language, a domain-speciﬁc
language (DSL) was devised to model these interactions
within the RESTful framework. This automation facilitates
the creation and execution of extensive simulations, with
predeﬁned ranges for critical parameters such as the number of
items and buffer sizes, enhancing the robustness of the dataset.

1289	mesh topologies, generating training data without requir-
1290	ing deployment on live infrastructure. Starting from simple
1291	tree-structured graphs and extending to general DAGs, we
1292	demonstrated how the framework scales across increasing
1293	architectural complexity.
1294	Graph Neural Networks allow us to capture both structural
1295	and feature-based dependencies in microservice interactions,
1296	achieving accurate system-level fault probability predictions.

1298	framework can highlight the most failure-prone microservices–
