The training dataset generation method and the volume of
generated samples ensure comprehensive coverage of potential
states and transitions, thereby obviating the necessity for noise
reduction. The framework’s methodological approach ensures
that the resultant dataset is both diverse and representative of
potential real-world RESTful service interactions, signiﬁcantly
contributing to the accuracy and reliability of subsequent
analyses and models.
The current approach prioritizes computational efﬁciency
and simpliﬁes the simulation of network dynamics by focusing
failures predominantly at the leaf nodes. This decision ensures
that the model remains scalable and manageable, particularly
when simulating extensive service meshes with multiple layers
of intermediate nodes. By using retry counters at intermediary

nodes, the model effectively emulates the robustness strategies
typical in contemporary cloud infrastructures, where fault
tolerance is largely handled through retries and load balancing
rather than expecting individual intermediaries to manage
failure. This abstraction aligns with industry practices, where
resilience is achieved through redundancy and failover mecha-
nisms, minimizing the need to simulate internal failures at all
node levels within the architecture.
Training datasets were generated based on the approach
described above. Several cases, each containing simulation
datasets, were generated for different architecture topologies
(based on random DAGs). These then were expanded with sets
of sub-cases, each with random parameter values for Pfail [m]
and retries[n] following a uniform distribution. For each case,
a graph description in Graph Exchange XML Format [44] was
augmented with these new node attributes.
As internal state graph transition state simulations were
considered less important in this phase of research, their length
was reduced to 10.000 steps. To aid experiments focusing on
the external observable properties of the cloud applications, a
new ﬁltered state simulation format was devised, as illustrated
by Table II. This message simulation dataset consists of the
following ﬁelds:
• id: event identiﬁer, the discrete timestamp of the logical
clock
• from: message source node identiﬁer in format Xn where
is n is the node identiﬁer
• to: message destination node identiﬁer in format Xn
• method: simulated HTTP method, only GET is imple-
mented at the time of writing
• action: simulated HTTP action, with values req for
requests and resp for responses
Fig. 8. Learning curve for fault probability prediction on tree-shaped service
meshes: validation R2 score (left axis) and validation MAE score (right axis)
over epochs (mean ± standard deviation across 3 runs).
• result: simulated HTTP result code for resp actions,
with values 2xx for normal responses, and 5xx for error
responses.
Based on the core model properties and node strategies
described in the previous section, the message patterns follow
a depth-ﬁrst walk pattern with optional back-tracking. This
means that for any given pair of communicating nodes, the
following statements hold true:
• for each req action there must be at least one resp action,
more resp actions are allowed in case of errors
• for each req action at least one resp action is mandatory,
so requests are not queued
At this phase of research, the total experimental dataset
volume has exceeded 2.1 GB, including cloud architecture
models in 50 cases for tree-shaped service meshes and 10 cases
for DAG-based service meshes, each with distinct topologies.
Each tree-shaped case contains 50 subcases, and each DAG-
based case contains 10 subcases. The graphs in the dataset
consist of 25 RESTful nodes per service mesh. While the
underlying graph structure remains the same within each
case, the node features–the number of retries for intermediary
nodes and the probability of failure for leaf nodes–vary across
subcases, offering a diverse set of conﬁgurations for analysis.
The calculated system-level fault probabilities in the dataset
range from a minimum of 0.0 to a maximum of 1.0, with a
median of 1.2e-5.
B. Fault Prediction Results on Tree-shaped Service Meshes
In this subsection, we present the results of our experiments
on tree-shaped service meshes. These experiments demonstrate
the model’s ability to capture both the relationships between
nodes and their connections, as well as how variations in
node features and the overall mesh structure inﬂuence system
reliability.

0.009± 0.001 on the test set, demonstrating strong generaliza-
tion across diverse tree-shaped service mesh topologies. The

Additionally, we examined the effect of varying the training
set size on model performance. As shown in Figure 9, the plot
presents the test R 2 score and test MAE score as functions of
the training set fraction. The ﬁgure shows that the test MAE
decreases consistently as the training set size increases, while

higher values. These results highlight the importance of using
a large and diverse dataset to enable the model to effectively
capture the underlying dependencies within the service mesh.
This is crucial for further analyses on identifying critical
components within the network.
C. Fault Prediction Results on DAG-Shaped Service Meshes
In this subsection, we extend our experiments to DAG-
shaped service meshes to evaluate the model’s ability to
generalize across more complex network topologies.
As shown in Figure 10, the learning curve for DAG-shaped
service meshes shows a pattern similar to that observed for
tree-shaped meshes, with a consistent decrease in the MAE
score and a corresponding increase in the validation R 2 score
over epochs. The best model on the validation set achieved a
test MAE of 0.009 ± 0.002, indicating strong generalization
across diverse DAG-shaped service mesh topologies. The

regression plot further conﬁrms the close alignment between
predicted and actual system fault probabilities, with a test R 2
score of 0.996± 0.003 (Figure 15, subﬁgure (a))).
We further evaluated the model trained on DAG-shaped
service meshes by testing it on the tree-shaped service mesh
dataset to assess its ability to transfer across different topolo-
gies. The pretrained model achieved a test MAE score of
0.038 ± 0.006 and a test R 2 score of 0.938 ± 0.014 on the
tree-shaped service mesh test set. These results, while slightly
lower than those of the model trained directly on tree-shaped
meshes, clearly demonstrate the model’s capacity to generalize
effectively across different service mesh structures.
As in our experiments on tree-shaped service meshes,
we explored the impact of varying the training set size on
the model’s performance. Figure 11 illustrates a clear trend:
increasing the training set size leads to a decreasing MAE
score and an increasing R 2 score on the test set, with both
metrics stabilizing at higher values. This consistency afﬁrms
our earlier conclusion that larger, more diverse datasets allow
the model to better capture the relationships within the service
mesh topology.
D. Baseline Comparison
To contextualize the performance of our GNN model and
to isolate the contributions of nonlinear transformations and
message passing, we implemented a systematic set of baseline
models:
• LinReg: We bucketized the node feature values into ﬁve
buckets per feature by sorting the values and dividing
them into equal-sized groups. The mean within each
bucket was computed, resulting in a permutation-invariant
representation that is independent of node ordering and
robust to variations in graph size. A linear regression
model was then ﬁt to these aggregated features.
• LinReg with spectral embeddings: Since linear regression
cannot capture the graph structure, we computed the
spectral embedding of each graph, applied the same
bucketization to the spectral coordinates, and concate-
nated these with the bucketized node features. A linear
regression model was ﬁt to the combined features.

• MLP: This model uses the same architecture as the GNN,
but with all message passing layers replaced by linear
layers. Permutation invariance is preserved through global
mean pooling, while the model loses the GNN’s ability
to capture node interactions through message passing.
• MLP with spectral embeddings: The same architecture as
above, but with spectral coordinates concatenated to the
node features. This provides information about the graph
structure in the absence of message passing.
Table III presents the test set MAE for each model on
tree- and DAG-shaped service meshes. The linear regres-
sion models achieve limited accuracy, even when spectral
embeddings are included, showing their inability to capture
complex interactions between nodes. The MLP baselines
provide improvements, particularly when spectral embeddings
are used, but still fall short of the GNN’s performance.
These results highlight the critical role of message passing in
effectively modeling node interactions. At the same time, they
illustrate the tradeoff between model complexity and inter-
pretability, motivating the explainability method introduced in
the next section.
VI. E XPERIMENT 2: D ETECTION OF CRITICAL
COMPONENTS WITH GNN E XPLAINABILITY
In this experiment, we focus on our core objective: iden-
tifying the critical components within service meshes using
GNN explainability techniques. By applying an explainability
method to a well-trained GNN model, we determine which
nodes (or subnetworks) have the most signiﬁcant inﬂuence on
the system’s overall reliability. This allows us to detect both
weak points and essential nodes whose failure or underper-
formance could severely impact service quality. This deeper
insight is crucial for improving service robustness, as it enables
targeted troubleshooting in the network’s most inﬂuential
areas. Additionally, this understanding lays the groundwork
for future work, where the cloud debugger system can be
steered toward potential failure points, enabling more effective
remediation and resilience testing.
A. Training Dataset
For this experiment, we used the same datasets as in the
fault prediction experiments, which consist of both tree-shaped
and DAG-shaped service meshes. These datasets allow us
to evaluate the model’s ability to detect critical components
across varying topologies and service conﬁgurations.

the R2 score for complementary nodes steadily decreases from 0.306 to 0.048
as more informative nodes are moved to the selected set. Similarly, the MAE
score for selected nodes remains low, while the MAE score for complementary

B. Explainability Results on Tree-Shaped Service Meshes
In this section, we present the explainability results for tree-
shaped service meshes. Using the predictor GNN, we applied
our explainability algorithm to identify which nodes are most
inﬂuential in predicting system fault situations, discovering the
critical components of the networks.
Figure 12 shows the regression results for the predictor
GNN on tree-shaped service meshes. The ﬁrst plot (a) illus-
trates the predictions made using all nodes in the service
mesh, which align very closely with the actual system fault
probabilities, achieving an R 2 score of 0.992± 0.005 on the
test set. This result indicates the model’s strong predictive
performance when using the full set of nodes in the network.
Plot (b) demonstrates the predictions made using only the
top 30% of nodes selected by the explainer network. Despite
reducing the input to a smaller subset, the model maintains
strong performance, achieving an R 2 score of 0.974± 0.018.
This is signiﬁcant, as it conﬁrms that these selected nodes
explain most of the variance in the predicted fault outcomes,
effectively identifying them as the most important components
for prediction. In contrast, plot (c) shows the predictions
made on the complementary 70% of nodes, where the R 2
score drops to 0.104± 0.042. This suggests that these nodes
provide minimal information about the fault outcomes, essen-
tially leading to a baseline mean prediction. The dramatic
drop in performance further reinforces the importance of the
selected 30% of nodes in accurately predicting the network’s
reliability.
These results show how well our explainability method
works, with the selected nodes being key to predicting fault
outcomes accurately. The sharp drop between the predictive
power of the selected and unselected nodes afﬁrms the power
of our method in identifying key components that drive
network reliability.
We further investigated how adjusting the selection budget,
i.e., the proportion of selected nodes, inﬂuences the model’s

To demonstrate better how our explainer network works,
we show a simple example in Figure 14 (a). In this example,
nodes are colored based on their selection probabilities, which
show how important each node is for predicting the fault
outcome. There is a leaf node next to the root with the
relatively high failure probability of 0.27 (marked in red).
Since this node is close to the root and has a high risk of
failure, it plays a key role in determining the overall system
fault probability. As a result, the ground truth system failure
probability is a high value of 0.93. Our explainer network
correctly identiﬁes this node as important, assigning it a
high selection probability. Using only the selected nodes, the
model predicts that system fault probability is 0.94, which
is very close to the actual value. In contrast, when the
predictor uses only the unselected nodes, the predicted system
fault probability is 0.02. This large difference shows that the
unselected nodes cannot be used to determine the fault. Most
of the unselected nodes are stable, and the leaves that could fail
are far from the root, where intermediary nodes can mitigate
if something goes wrong.
In Figure 14 (b), we changed the example slightly by
setting the failure probability of this critical leaf node next
to the root to 0.0. This leads to a signiﬁcant change in the
predicted system fault probability. Using the selected nodes,
the predicted system fault probability drops to 0.0 because the
critical node no longer has a risk of failure. The predicted
system fault probability for the unselected nodes stays the
same. This result is what we would expect and conﬁrms that
the explainer works correctly.
In Figure 14 (c), we made another slight change by moving
the critical leaf node to a lower level in the service mesh,
attaching it to an intermediary node that can retry once after
a failure. This change affects how the explainer behaves: now
only this critical node gets selected. As we expected, the
predicted system fault probability drops to 0.01 due to the
recovery capability of the intermediary node, which can retry
the request if a failure occurs.
C. Explainability Results on DAG-Shaped Service Meshes
In this subsection, we extend our explainability analysis to
DAG-shaped service meshes. As with the tree-shaped meshes,
we used the predictor GNN and applied the explainability
algorithm to determine which nodes were most critical for
predicting the system fault outcomes.
Figure 15 presents the regression results for the DAG-
shaped service meshes. In plot (a), we see the predictions
made using all nodes in the network. The predictor closely
aligns with the true system fault probabilities, achieving an
R2 score of 0.996± 0.003, showing that the model performs
exceptionally well when considering the entire set of nodes.

maintains a strong performance, with an R 2 score of 0.861±

the critical information for fault prediction. In contrast, plot

explainer may sometimes overlook sparse but highly informa-
tive components, and could beneﬁt from further ﬁne-tuning or
regularization to increase robustness.
VII. D ISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
Designing dependable and scalable cloud services requires
systematic tools to analyze complex behaviors and iden-
tify faults efﬁciently. While many existing approaches in
the literature target speciﬁc aspects of fault detection–
such as networking faults, security breaches, or system-level
anomalies–they often operate at a ﬁxed abstraction level
and lack generalizability across cloud environments. This
work contributes a uniﬁed and explainable approach to fault

forecasting in microservice-based cloud systems, using prob-
abilistic modeling and graph-based machine learning.
Our proposed method combines a formally veriﬁed sim-
ulation environment with data-driven fault prediction and
explainability. The use of the PRISM model checker enables
us to simulate fault propagation across a variety of service
mesh topologies, generating training data without requir-
ing deployment on live infrastructure. Starting from simple
tree-structured graphs and extending to general DAGs, we
demonstrated how the framework scales across increasing
architectural complexity.
Graph Neural Networks allow us to capture both structural
and feature-based dependencies in microservice interactions,
achieving accurate system-level fault probability predictions.
Furthermore, by integrating an explainability mechanism, the
framework can highlight the most failure-prone microservices–
guiding debugging efforts toward critical components and
improving system-level fault understanding.
Although the current evaluation is based on synthetic
datasets to ensure full control and formal validation, real-
world applicability remains a priority. Future work will focus
on integrating real-world cloud traces, adapting to dynamic
operational environments, and extending the method to broader
observability contexts.

# Explainable GNN-Based Approach to Fault Forecasting (Unyi et al., TNSM 2025)

> Notes from the **full text** (`litdb/texts/unyi2025explainable.txt`). Page numbers are PDF pages (journal pp.5640-5657). Figures not inspected; Table III cell values did not extract.

## 1. Summary
A GNN is trained to predict the system-level failure probability of a synthetic service mesh (random 25-node trees and DAGs) from two node features: leaf failure probability and intermediary retry count. Labels come from the PRISM probabilistic model checker. An explainer GNN trained with REINFORCE picks a subset of nodes (10-50% budget) that preserves prediction accuracy. No real telemetry is used.

## 2. Problem and motivation
- Debugging distributed services is reactive and partially observable (pp.1-2). Argued from citations; no incident data.

## 3. Method (pp.3-9)
- PRISM generates MDPs from random DAGs; the label is a model-checked probability of root failure (Pmax) (p.7).
- Predictor: four message-passing blocks (hidden 32), mean pool, 200 epochs, Adam 2e-4, MSE, 80/10/10 random split over meshes (p.8).
- Explainer: Bernoulli node mask, reward = MSE(complement) - MSE(selected) + sparsity term (p.9).

## 4. Data and setup (p.10-11)
- 50 tree topologies x 50 parameter subcases, 10 DAG topologies x 10 subcases, 25 nodes each; fault probabilities range 0.0 to 1.0, median 1.2e-5 (p.11).
- Random split is at the mesh level; subcases of the same topology share a topology, so mesh-level random splits put near-identical graph structures in train and test (my inference from the case/subcase structure).

## 5. Results (copied)
| Metric | Theirs | Best baseline | Baseline name | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tree meshes test MAE / R2 | 0.009 +/- 0.001 / 0.992 +/- 0.005 | not extracted | LinReg, MLP variants | pp.11-13 |
| DAG meshes test MAE / R2 | 0.009 +/- 0.002 / 0.996 +/- 0.003 | not extracted | same | p.12 |
| DAG-trained model tested on trees | MAE 0.038 +/- 0.006, R2 0.938 +/- 0.014 | n/a | n/a | p.12 |
| Explainer 30% nodes, tree / DAG | R2 0.974 +/- 0.018 / 0.861 +/- 0.054 | complement 0.104 / 0.072 | n/a | pp.13-15 |
- Baseline MAE values are in Table III (p.13) as an image; text says MLP with spectral embeddings is better than linear regression but below the GNN.

## 6. Limitations
- Stated: synthetic data only; real traces left to future work; explainer sometimes masks critical sparse nodes (pp.15-16).
- **My critique:**
  1. "Fault forecasting" here is regression of a model-checker output from the very parameters that define the label (leaf failure probabilities and retries). The GNN approximates a known reliability computation, so R2 near 0.99 shows it learned a formula, not that it forecasts real failures.
  2. No real traces, metrics or logs; transfer to real systems is untested (the paper says so, p.16).
  3. Only three runs per setting; no significance tests; random mesh-level splits with shared topologies across subcases.
  4. The explainer finds nodes that matter for a synthetic formula (leaf near the root, few retries), which is largely implied by the generator.
  5. Median fault probability 1.2e-5 means most targets are near zero, so high R2 and low MAE are dominated by easy cases; MAE 0.009 is not scale-free (no relative error reported).
  6. Authors disclose use of ChatGPT and Grammarly for text (p.15).
- Not discussed: calibration, class-imbalanced evaluation of high-risk meshes, comparison with a closed-form or Monte Carlo estimator.

## 7. Reproducibility
- Dataset and code stated at github.com/BME-SmartLab/GNN-Fault-Forecasting (not checked or run).

## 8. Comparison with OUR work
| Dimension | This paper | Ours (rca-lab) | Who is stronger, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Label requirement | simulator labels | none | ours |
| Live / streaming | no | incremental windows | ours |
| Telemetry used | none | traces (+ metrics) | ours |
| Propagation modelling | GNN on a retry/MDP model | edge probabilities | theirs richer; synthetic |
| Forecasts future failures | system fault probability from node parameters | claimed, untested | neither on real data |
| Explanation | critical node subgraph | templates | theirs (on synthetic) |
| Evaluation rigor | synthetic, 3 runs | synthetic | neither |
| Open / reproducible | stated | yes | tie |

- **What they have that we do not:** an explainer that selects a necessary and sufficient node subset.
- **What we have that they do not:** real telemetry and RCA scoring; negative controls.
- **Could a reviewer say "this already exists"?** Not for real-telemetry cascade risk; yes for "GNN predicts failure probability from a service graph" in simulation.
- **Position:** cite as simulation-based related work on graph-level fault probability prediction. It is not evidence of real forecasting performance.
- **Must we run it as a baseline?** No.

## 9. Does this paper change what problem we should solve?
- It does not change the problem. It shows that "GNN fault forecasting" papers exist that never touch real telemetry; our paper can state that real-trace cascade forecasting remains untested in this line.
- It also corrects my earlier note: the TNSM 2025 "fault forecasting" paper is simulation-only.

## 10. Citation-ready facts (each with page)
- "A GNN reached R2 0.992 (tree) and 0.996 (DAG) predicting model-checker fault probabilities on synthetic 25-node service meshes" (pp.11-12).
- "The authors state real-world evaluation is future work" (p.16).

## 11. Open questions / things to verify
- Table III values; repository contents; Scopus status of ISSN 1932-4537.

50	ABSTRACT
51	In the AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) era, accu-
52	rately forecasting system states is crucial. In microservices systems,
53	this task encounters the challenge of dynamic and complex spatio-
54	temporal relationships among microservice instances, primarily
55	due to dynamic deployments, diverse call paths, and cascading ef-
56	fects among instances. Current time-series forecasting methods,
57	which focus mainly on intrinsic patterns, are insufficient in envi-
58	ronments where spatial relationships are critical. Similarly, spatio-
59	temporal graph approaches often neglect the nature of temporal
60	trend, concentrating mostly on message passing between nodes.
61	Moreover, current research in microservices domain frequently
62	underestimates the importance of network metrics and topological
63	structures in capturing the evolving dynamics of systems. This pa-
64	per introduces STMformer, a model tailored for forecasting system
65	states in microservices environments, capable of handling multi-
66	node and multivariate time series. Our method leverages dynamic
67	network connection data and topological information to assist in
68	modeling the intricate spatio-temporal relationships within the
69	system. Additionally, we integrate the PatchCrossAttention module
70	to compute the impact of cascading effects globally. We have de-
71	veloped a dataset based on a microservices system and conducted

100	1 INTRODUCTION
101	With the rapid advancement of cloud-native technology, the struc-
102	tural paradigm of cloud applications is transitioning from large
103	monolithic services to distributed microservices systems[1]. In pro-
104	duction deployments, these microservices could be containerized
105	and deployed over IT infrastructure, greatly expanding the sys-
106	tem’s vulnerability to both failures and security[ 8, 25, 32]. The
107	escalating complexity and scale of cloud data centers and the grow-
108	ing pressures on SREs(Site Reliability Engineers) are driving the
109	shift towards AIOps(Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) in
110	industry[19]. In the domain of intelligent IT operations, accurate
111	prediction of future system states is essential for downstream tasks,
112	such as anomaly detection and resource allocation, which could
113	grant sufficient time for decision-making and strategy execution[5,
114	arXiv:2408.07894v1  [cs.NI]  15 Aug 2024
115	=== page 2 ===
116	Conference’24, July, 2024 Yifei Xu et al.
117	(a)
118	 (b)
119	Figure 1: (a) shows multiple relationships in the microservices system. The blue circles represents the observation metrics of
120	pod. (b) shows instance metrics of ts-seat-service and ts-order-service under two fault injections. First row shows network loss
121	faults and second row shows CPU stress faults.
122	26]. It epitomizes the sophisticated integration of AI into opera-
123	tional frameworks, emphasizing proactive measures in the dynamic
124	and complex situation of cloud native technologies.
125	As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), microservice instances are container-
126	ized and deployed on nodes (either virtual or physical machines),
127	and these instances are interconnected through network commu-
128	nications that establish dependency relationships, which results
129	in instance states being influenced by neighboring instances in
130	both spatial and temporal dimensions. Fundamentally, system state
131	prediction is a multivariate time series forecasting problem. As
132	research in this field progresses, the current mainstream trend
133	is towards deep learning methods. Informer[40], Autoformer[34],
134	and Fedformer[41] explore relationships between time steps from
135	the time or frequency domain and focus on reducing the com-
136	putational complexity of the attention mechanism. TimesNet[33]
137	captures sequence features within and between time series cy-
138	cles. PatchTST[20] introduces patch operations into time series,
139	enabling the new time-step sequences to contain local informa-
140	tion. While these approaches are dedicated to capturing temporal
141	trends, they often lack modeling of the spatial dependencies be-
142	tween instances data. On the other hand, the spatial relationships
143	between instances allow the microservices system to be viewed
144	as a directed graph, enabling predictions using spatio-temporal
145	graph algorithms. STSGCN[29] constructs a new adjacency matrix
146	to simultaneously model spatio-temporal relationships within local
147	time steps. Building on this, STSGT[ 2] makes enhancements for
148	global time steps, but it still ignores relationships between nodes
149	from node perspective and the historical time steps of the input
150	sequences are notably short.
151	In addition to the issues with existing research methods, the
152	inherent complexity of microservices systems also leads to certain
153	limitations in conducting predictive tasks within this domain. These
154	limitations include: (1) instances on the same node(e.g., pod1 and
155	pod2 in Fig. 1(a)) can impact each other’s performance through
156	resource competition and network congestion[10, 27]. Moreover,
157	microservices deployed on platforms such as OpenShift[ 22] and
158	Kubernetes[12] exhibit dynamism, with service instances frequently
159	scaled, destroyed, and rebuilt based on demand, disrupting predic-
160	tion outcomes due to changes in deployment structures; (2) the
161	state of microservice instances is influenced not only by the inter-
162	relationships among multivariate variables within the instance but
163	also by the performance status of the nodes[15, 24, 31]. However,
164	existing research[6, 7, 14, 39] either employs simplistic network
165	metrics or overlooks node metrics altogether, which are insufficient
166	for aiding in the prediction of critical performance indicators. In the
167	right part of Fig. 1(b), the additional network metrics(green lines)
168	exhibited periodic fluctuations following the injection of faults. (3)
169	each access request has a unique call chain, leading to states being
170	influenced by continually changing requests. Static network topol-
171	ogy information is inadequate for adapting to the dynamic nature
172	of microservices systems. Moreover, the connection information
173	constructed from trace data lacks the necessary network metrics
174	we require for effective analysis; (4) cascading effects exist within
175	the microservices system, where an anomaly in one instance or a
176	surge in requests can impact upstream and downstream instances.
177	thereby increasing the complexity of spatio-temporal modeling. As
178	the second row of the Fig. 1(b) shows, CPU usage(blue lines) of
179	ts-order-service occurs delayed fluctuation when we inject CPU
180	stress faults into its adjacent service, ts-seat-service.
181	Unlike existing studies that use only past observations as in-
182	put, we believe that additional information can help improve the
183	accuracy of predictions. Therefore, in addition to extra network
184	metrics mentioned above, dynamic topological structure informa-
185	tion and adjacency matrices are also essential for predicting system
186	states. Based on OpenTelemetry[23], trace data, which could map
187	the sequence of service or function calls per request, can be col-
188	lected through distributed tracing tools like Zipkin[42], Jaeger[9],
189	and Skywalking[28], and can be used to generate dynamic connec-
190	tion information. These tools are crucial for visualizing service call
191	chains, providing a foundation for system analysis. However, de-
192	ploying these solutions faces obstacles. A survey[13] suggests high
193	costs may deter small companies from adoption. Some tools need to
194	invade source code for event tracking or support limited program-
195	ming languages. Moreover, trace data, which reflects application-
196	level information, fails to capture deeper operational data of in-
197	stances, pointing to the need for more comprehensive monitoring
198	approaches that combine application interactions with detailed sys-
199	tem metrics for a complete view of microservices’ performance. To
200	=== page 3 ===
201	System States Forecasting of Microservices with Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Data Conference’24, July, 2024
202	satisfy the aforementioned needs, we have developed a code-free in-
203	trusive tool that gathers status information for instances and nodes,
204	along with topological structure information. It utilizes eBPF[4] to
205	trace TCP connections, providing extensive network connection
206	details and dynamic adjacent matrices.
207	In this study, for system states forecasting tasks, we propose the
208	Spatio-Temporal Message Transformer-based model, STMformer,
209	to address the four previously mentioned challenges: 1) utilizing
210	dynamic topological information to address the dynamic deploy-
211	ment characteristics of microservices, 2) using rich network and
212	node metrics to overcome issues related to insufficient information,
213	3) employing captured network connection data to construct time-
214	varying adjacency matrices, which assist in accommodating the
215	dynamic changes of microservices instances, and 4) proposing a
216	solution from a global spatio-temporal perspective to address the
217	problem of cascading effect propagation. Our contributions in this
218	paper are listed as follows:
219	• We propose a model, STMformer, that utilizes dynamic topo-
220	logical structure information and network connections as
221	auxiliary data. It models the complex spatio-temporal re-
222	lationships from four perspectives to predict states of the
223	microservices system in both short-term and long-term fore-
224	casting tasks.
225	• To compute the propagation impacts of cascading effects
226	within the system from a global spatio-temporal perspective,
227	we introduce the PatchCrossAttention module. This module
228	performs attention calculations simultaneously across all
229	time spans of the state sequence and the global topological
230	structure at each time step.
231	• Based on an open resource microservices benchmark, we
232	have generated a dataset containing instances and nodes
233	state metrics, dynamic adjacent matrices and topology infor-
234	mation. And we evaluate our model against advanced time
235	series methods and spatio-temporal graph methods based
236	on the dataset, achieving superior performance compared
237	to state-of-the-art approaches in short-term and long-term
238	forecasting tasks.
239	This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 gives an overview
240	of the related works. Section 3 details the preliminaries of this
241	paper, and illustrates the structure of our proposed model. Section
242	4 describes experiments and results, and Section 5 summarizes our
243	conclusions and outlines future work.
244	2 RELATED WORK
245	2.1 Time Series Forecasting
246	Time series forecasting emerges as an exceptionally challenging
247	field, requiring a deep understanding of inherent characteristics
248	within temporal trends to predict future outcomes. This discipline
249	demands rigorous analysis and the application of sophisticated mod-
250	els to decode the intricate patterns embedded in time-dependent
251	data, enabling accurate projections of future states. Informer[40]
252	selects top-k weights in attention matrix based on KL-divergence,
253	achieving a substantial reduction in computational complexity and
254	memory usage. Autoformer[34] presents a novel approach by re-
255	placing the conventional self-attention mechanism with an Auto-
256	Correlation function by selecting top-k correlations in correlation
257	matrix. This ingenious substitution exploits the periodic nature
258	of series to identify and aggregate similar sub-series across dif-
259	ferent periods. Both Informer and Autoformer reduce the compu-
260	tational complexity to𝑂(𝐿 log𝐿). Fedformer[41] employs Fourier
261	and wavelet transformations for enhanced time series analysis,
262	achieving linear complexity and memory efficiency by selectively
263	incorporating crucial frequency components for a holistic repre-
264	sentation. TimesNet[33] proposes a novel approach by identifying
265	the top-k frequencies through Fourier transform and transform-
266	ing 1D time series data into a 2D space. By leveraging 2D con-
267	volutional operations, it captures the temporal variation patterns
268	both within and across different frequency cycles. This method-
269	ology achieves optimal performance in a variety of time series
270	tasks, including forecasting, imputation, classification, and anom-
271	aly detection, demonstrating its comprehensive applicability and
272	effectiveness in extracting complex temporal dynamics.
273	2.2 Spatio-Temporal Graph
274	When temporal data also contains spatial relationships, simply
275	analyzing time trends is insufficient. Viewing this kind of data as a
276	spatio-temporal graph has proven beneficial, especially in traffic and
277	weather forecasting, highlighting the importance of considering
278	both spatial and temporal dimensions in predictive analysis.
279	STAD[36] leverage detailed component topology and metric de-
280	pendencies, integrating dynamic time warping with graph neural
281	networks to capture spatial relationships and temporal dynam-
282	ics within cloud environments. STSGCN[29] innovatively captures
283	localized spatio-temporal correlations and heterogeneities in spatio-
284	temporal data. Unlike previous methods, STSGCN synchronously
285	processes spatial and temporal data through a unified framework,
286	demonstrating superior forecasting performance on real-world
287	datasets. STGIN[17] introduces a spatio-temporal Transformer-
288	based model for long-term traffic forecasting, integrating Graph
289	Attention Network(GAT) and Informer layers to effectively capture
290	the spatial and temporal dependencies of traffic data. However,
291	it relies on static spatial topology for its adjacency matrix and
292	does not incorporate real-time connectivity information into the
293	model. MGT[37] innovatively integrates meta-learning with atten-
294	tion mechanisms to model spatio-temporal heterogeneity. But its
295	algorithm heavily relies on for loops, and in the Decoder phase,
296	it adopts a single time-step loop inference, which substantially
297	slows down the model’s computational speed. Consequently, spatio-
298	temporal methods more focus on message passing between nodes,
299	neglecting the intrinsic patterns of the time series.
300	3 METHODOLOGY
301	3.1 Problem Statement
302	To elucidate the spatial and temporal dependencies and influences
303	among instances within a microservices system, our framework in-
304	tegrates state metrics with network adjacent matrices and topology
305	information data, enabling us to conceptualize the system architec-

ABSTRACT
In the AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) era, accu-
rately forecasting system states is crucial. In microservices systems,
this task encounters the challenge of dynamic and complex spatio-
temporal relationships among microservice instances, primarily
due to dynamic deployments, diverse call paths, and cascading ef-
fects among instances. Current time-series forecasting methods,
which focus mainly on intrinsic patterns, are insufficient in envi-
ronments where spatial relationships are critical. Similarly, spatio-
temporal graph approaches often neglect the nature of temporal
trend, concentrating mostly on message passing between nodes.
Moreover, current research in microservices domain frequently
underestimates the importance of network metrics and topological
structures in capturing the evolving dynamics of systems. This pa-
per introduces STMformer, a model tailored for forecasting system
states in microservices environments, capable of handling multi-
node and multivariate time series. Our method leverages dynamic
network connection data and topological information to assist in
modeling the intricate spatio-temporal relationships within the
system. Additionally, we integrate the PatchCrossAttention module
to compute the impact of cascading effects globally. We have de-
veloped a dataset based on a microservices system and conducted

1 INTRODUCTION
With the rapid advancement of cloud-native technology, the struc-
tural paradigm of cloud applications is transitioning from large
monolithic services to distributed microservices systems[1]. In pro-
duction deployments, these microservices could be containerized
and deployed over IT infrastructure, greatly expanding the sys-
tem’s vulnerability to both failures and security[ 8, 25, 32]. The
escalating complexity and scale of cloud data centers and the grow-
ing pressures on SREs(Site Reliability Engineers) are driving the

As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), microservice instances are container-
ized and deployed on nodes (either virtual or physical machines),
and these instances are interconnected through network commu-
nications that establish dependency relationships, which results
in instance states being influenced by neighboring instances in
both spatial and temporal dimensions. Fundamentally, system state
prediction is a multivariate time series forecasting problem. As
research in this field progresses, the current mainstream trend
is towards deep learning methods. Informer[40], Autoformer[34],
and Fedformer[41] explore relationships between time steps from
the time or frequency domain and focus on reducing the com-
putational complexity of the attention mechanism. TimesNet[33]
captures sequence features within and between time series cy-
cles. PatchTST[20] introduces patch operations into time series,
enabling the new time-step sequences to contain local informa-
tion. While these approaches are dedicated to capturing temporal
trends, they often lack modeling of the spatial dependencies be-
tween instances data. On the other hand, the spatial relationships
between instances allow the microservices system to be viewed
as a directed graph, enabling predictions using spatio-temporal
graph algorithms. STSGCN[29] constructs a new adjacency matrix
to simultaneously model spatio-temporal relationships within local
time steps. Building on this, STSGT[ 2] makes enhancements for
global time steps, but it still ignores relationships between nodes
from node perspective and the historical time steps of the input
sequences are notably short.
In addition to the issues with existing research methods, the
inherent complexity of microservices systems also leads to certain
limitations in conducting predictive tasks within this domain. These
limitations include: (1) instances on the same node(e.g., pod1 and
pod2 in Fig. 1(a)) can impact each other’s performance through
resource competition and network congestion[10, 27]. Moreover,
microservices deployed on platforms such as OpenShift[ 22] and
Kubernetes[12] exhibit dynamism, with service instances frequently
scaled, destroyed, and rebuilt based on demand, disrupting predic-
tion outcomes due to changes in deployment structures; (2) the
state of microservice instances is influenced not only by the inter-
relationships among multivariate variables within the instance but
also by the performance status of the nodes[15, 24, 31]. However,
existing research[6, 7, 14, 39] either employs simplistic network

of microservices systems. Moreover, the connection information
constructed from trace data lacks the necessary network metrics
we require for effective analysis; (4) cascading effects exist within
the microservices system, where an anomaly in one instance or a
surge in requests can impact upstream and downstream instances.

• We propose a model, STMformer, that utilizes dynamic topo-

2 RELATED WORK
2.1 Time Series Forecasting
Time series forecasting emerges as an exceptionally challenging
field, requiring a deep understanding of inherent characteristics
within temporal trends to predict future outcomes. This discipline
demands rigorous analysis and the application of sophisticated mod-
els to decode the intricate patterns embedded in time-dependent
data, enabling accurate projections of future states. Informer[40]
selects top-k weights in attention matrix based on KL-divergence,
achieving a substantial reduction in computational complexity and
memory usage. Autoformer[34] presents a novel approach by re-
placing the conventional self-attention mechanism with an Auto-
Correlation function by selecting top-k correlations in correlation
matrix. This ingenious substitution exploits the periodic nature
of series to identify and aggregate similar sub-series across dif-
ferent periods. Both Informer and Autoformer reduce the compu-
tational complexity to𝑂(𝐿 log𝐿). Fedformer[41] employs Fourier
and wavelet transformations for enhanced time series analysis,
achieving linear complexity and memory efficiency by selectively
incorporating crucial frequency components for a holistic repre-
sentation. TimesNet[33] proposes a novel approach by identifying
the top-k frequencies through Fourier transform and transform-
ing 1D time series data into a 2D space. By leveraging 2D con-
volutional operations, it captures the temporal variation patterns
both within and across different frequency cycles. This method-
ology achieves optimal performance in a variety of time series
tasks, including forecasting, imputation, classification, and anom-
aly detection, demonstrating its comprehensive applicability and
effectiveness in extracting complex temporal dynamics.
2.2 Spatio-Temporal Graph
When temporal data also contains spatial relationships, simply
analyzing time trends is insufficient. Viewing this kind of data as a
spatio-temporal graph has proven beneficial, especially in traffic and
weather forecasting, highlighting the importance of considering
both spatial and temporal dimensions in predictive analysis.
STAD[36] leverage detailed component topology and metric de-
pendencies, integrating dynamic time warping with graph neural
networks to capture spatial relationships and temporal dynam-
ics within cloud environments. STSGCN[29] innovatively captures
localized spatio-temporal correlations and heterogeneities in spatio-
temporal data. Unlike previous methods, STSGCN synchronously
processes spatial and temporal data through a unified framework,
demonstrating superior forecasting performance on real-world
datasets. STGIN[17] introduces a spatio-temporal Transformer-
based model for long-term traffic forecasting, integrating Graph
Attention Network(GAT) and Informer layers to effectively capture
the spatial and temporal dependencies of traffic data. However,
it relies on static spatial topology for its adjacency matrix and
does not incorporate real-time connectivity information into the
model. MGT[37] innovatively integrates meta-learning with atten-
tion mechanisms to model spatio-temporal heterogeneity. But its
algorithm heavily relies on for loops, and in the Decoder phase,
it adopts a single time-step loop inference, which substantially
slows down the model’s computational speed. Consequently, spatio-
temporal methods more focus on message passing between nodes,
neglecting the intrinsic patterns of the time series.

analysis of the intricate interplay between various instances, un-
derscoring the critical role of state, network events and topology
in understanding the dynamic behavior of microservices.

PatchCrossAttention(PCA) In the intricate landscape of mi-
croservice architectures, a fault or surge in one service on the call
chain does not immediately impact its upstream or downstream
counterparts. Instead, there exists a delay in the propagation of

nodes across multiple hops may be affected after a more extended

perspectives: one from the node perspective and the other from
the edge perspective. From the node perspective, it is crucial for a
single node to engage in attention mechanism computations with
all nodes across multiple time steps. However, this requirement can
lead to substantial computational overhead and may not effectively
correlate trends across time steps. From the edge perspective, we
consider constructing a global spatio-temporal adjacency matrix to
refine the computational attention results of the nodes.

4 EXPERIMENT
In this section, we will discuss data collection and processing, pro-
vide an overview of the benchmark model, and analyze the results
of comparative experiments, ablation studies, and hyperparameter
studies.
4.1 Dataset
Based on the coroot-node-agent[21], we developed an distributed
metrics collector to obtain the data we need. The collector could
not only integrate eBPF programs, enabling the tracking of TCP
connection events among instances, including but not limited to
connection establishment, listening, drop and retransmission ac-
tivities, but also record metrics of pods and nodes with cgroup
technique. We define more than 80 kinds of metrics, including CPU
usage, memory usage, disk I/O stats, connection latency, span of
TCP states transferring, length of socket queue and throughput of
sockets and so on.

856	4.4 Overall Performance
857	To comprehensively evaluate the performance of our model in
858	system state prediction tasks, we conducted experiments for both
859	short-term and long-term forecasting and compared them with
860	benchmark models. Table 1 displays the results of the short-term
861	forecasting tasks, while Table 2 shows the results of the long-term
862	forecasting tasks.
863	Based on the experimental results, we can draw the following
864	conclusions: (1) In short-term forecasting tasks, our model out-
865	performs other benchmark models. In long-term tasks, our model
866	slightly surpasses PatchTST in some metrics while generally per-
867	forming better than the benchmark models. Our model improves
868	upon the next best model by 8.6% in MAE and 2.2% in MSE. (2) Time
869	series models demonstrate superior performance in capturing tem-
870	poral trends, but they lack modeling of spatial relationships, which
871	significantly impacts system state prediction tasks for microser-
872	vices. The results from TimesNet exceed those of our model, and
873	our use of the TimesBlock module in our model indicates that the
874	inability to transfer spatial information between nodes affects the
875	task outcomes. (3) Spatio-temporal graph models generally show
876	poor performance, especially the STSGT model, which exhibits
877	non-convergence issues at strides of 16 and 64. The main reason
878	could be that it does not consider the correlation of node states
879	at different time steps from the perspective of the nodes them-
880	selves, but only performs message passing from the perspective
881	of the edges. Meanwhile, STSGCN shows performance similar to
882	Informer but fails to capture intrinsic patterns of the time series,
883	hence its performance is lower than our model. Finally, STMformer
884	can accurately capture dynamic features in spatio-temporal data
885	and effectively compensates for the shortcomings of these methods,
886	thereby achieving superior performance.

958	4.6 Hyperparameter Studies
959	Changes in the hyperparameters of the STMformer typically affect
960	model’s predictive performance. To validate the impact of hyperpa-
961	rameters on the STMformer, we will analyze from five perspectives:
962	the dimension of the model, the choice of kernel length for sequence
963	decomposition, the number of attention heads, the ProbSparseAt-
964	tention factor, and the hyperparameters of the TB-PCA module.
965	As the Fig. 4(a) shows, changes in model parameters significantly
966	affect the performance of the STMformer. As the dimensions of
967	model parameters increase, the performance of the model improves.
968	This indicates that a higher-dimensional vector space enhances the
969	model’s learning capabilities. Node states, after being processed
970	through various spatio-temporal relationship calculations, implic-
971	itly contain elements of physical spatial deployment, spatial logical
972	relationships, trends in time series, and global spatio-temporal re-
973	lationships. Enhancing model parameters helps nodes learn these
974	complex features. Fig. 4(b) illustrates that the model is influenced
975	by the choice of kernel for sequence decomposition. The optimal
976	selection of kernel length depends on the pattern fluctuations of
977	the time series and expert experience. Choosing the appropriate
978	set of kernel lengths can more accurately obtain trends, allowing
979	the model to focus on learning the remaining parts of the series.
980	The Fig. 4(c) and Fig. 4(d) display experiments related to attention-
981	related hyperparameters. The choice of the number of attention
982	heads, if too large or too small, affects the model’s performance,

1004	5 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
1005	For predicting the state of microservices systems, we developed the
1006	STMformer model, which leverages dynamically derived adjacency
1007	matrices from network events and deployment structures to cap-
1008	ture spatio-temporal relationships characteristic of microservices
1009	systems. We also design PatchCrossAttention module to analyze
1010	cascading effects from a global spatio-temporal perspective. Our ex-
1011	periments show that STMformer outperforms benchmark methods,
1012	confirming the effectiveness of its components and the influence of
1013	hyperparameters on its performance. Our future work will focus on
1014	reducing computational complexity, automating kernel generation
1015	for sequence decomposition, and integrating multimodal data for
1016	more robust microservices system representations.

loads, we adjusted concurrent user numbers and utilized chaos-

specific faults. This process enabled the collection of detailed sys-

insights into the system’s resilience and behavior under stress. We

record metrics every 5 seconds and spent 1 to 2 hours under dif-
ferent conditions. Then we sort and aggregate data from nodes by
time stamp. Taking long-term forecasting as example, the dataset
covers about 14000 samples, every sample is an array consisting 64
time steps, 56 pods and 80 features.
Our deployed benchmark is an open-source experimental system
whose components have not undergone production-level testing.
As a result, under high concurrency and fault injection conditions,
system stability cannot be guaranteed, potentially leading to ex-
treme values in network observation data. To speed up computation
convergence, we apply log1p to network-relevant metrics and use
min-max normalization to scale data to[0, 1], both of which are
reversible processes.
4.2 Baselines
We compare our proposed STMformer against eight baseline mod-
els on short-term and long-term system states forecasting tasks.
The baseline models can be divided into two main categories de-
pending on how they process time series. The first category inte-
grates the metrics of all instances, ignoring the spatial relationship,
which means the input size is𝑋∈ R𝑇×𝑁𝐶 . It includes Informer[40],
Autoformer[34], FEDformer[41], PatchTST[20], TimesNet[33], and
DLinear[38]. The second category are spatio-temporal methods,
considering temporal and spatial relationship between instances,
such as STSGCN[29] and STSGT[2]. Its input size is𝑋∈ R𝑇×𝑁×𝐶.
• Informer: A Transformer-based model using ProbSparseAt-
tention and distillation to accelerate computation for time
series prediction.
• Autoformer: A Transformer-based model using series de-
composition and auto correlation to capture pattern of time
trend.
• FEDformer: A Transformer-based model selecting compo-
nents randomly to represent time series and calculating at-
tention in frequency domain.
• PatchTST: A Transformer-based model using patching to
aggregate local information from time series and perform
channel-independence computation.
• TimesNet: A CNN-based model leveraging FFT to find top-k
the most relevant frequencies and applying CNN on time
series by capturing time pattern within or across various
cycles.
• DLinear: A Linear model for time series prediction.
• STSGCN: A GCN-based model by using localized spatio-
temporal subgraph module to find localized correlations in-
dependently.
• STSGT: A model uses GCN to apply spatial message pass-
ing and calculates attention by building a spatial-temporal
synchronous graph among all nodes and time steps.

4.3 Experiment Setups
Train Ticket microservices are deployed on seven virtual machines,
each of which has a 8 GB RAM with system version Ubuntu 20.04.5
LTS. Each model is trained on a single NVIDIA A100 80G GPUs.
Dataset of all categories are divided into training sets, validation
sets, and test sets in a 8:1:1 ratio during modeling. We set the horizon
steps same as prediction steps. And we conduct short-term and
long-term prediction experiments on step size𝐿𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑟𝑡 =[16, 32] and
𝐿𝑙𝑜𝑛𝑔 =[64, 128] respectively. All transformer-based model are set
up to contain 3 encoder layers and 1 decoder layer. For detail of
training, model is refined by MSE loss and ADAM optimizer. We
also use gradient accumulation and warming up strategy for small
batches training, since each sample is a 3-dimension array.
4.4 Overall Performance
To comprehensively evaluate the performance of our model in
system state prediction tasks, we conducted experiments for both
short-term and long-term forecasting and compared them with
benchmark models. Table 1 displays the results of the short-term
forecasting tasks, while Table 2 shows the results of the long-term
forecasting tasks.
Based on the experimental results, we can draw the following
conclusions: (1) In short-term forecasting tasks, our model out-
performs other benchmark models. In long-term tasks, our model
slightly surpasses PatchTST in some metrics while generally per-
forming better than the benchmark models. Our model improves
upon the next best model by 8.6% in MAE and 2.2% in MSE. (2) Time
series models demonstrate superior performance in capturing tem-
poral trends, but they lack modeling of spatial relationships, which
significantly impacts system state prediction tasks for microser-
vices. The results from TimesNet exceed those of our model, and
our use of the TimesBlock module in our model indicates that the
inability to transfer spatial information between nodes affects the
task outcomes. (3) Spatio-temporal graph models generally show
poor performance, especially the STSGT model, which exhibits
non-convergence issues at strides of 16 and 64. The main reason
could be that it does not consider the correlation of node states
at different time steps from the perspective of the nodes them-
selves, but only performs message passing from the perspective
of the edges. Meanwhile, STSGCN shows performance similar to
Informer but fails to capture intrinsic patterns of the time series,
hence its performance is lower than our model. Finally, STMformer
can accurately capture dynamic features in spatio-temporal data
and effectively compensates for the shortcomings of these methods,
thereby achieving superior performance.
4.5 Ablation Studies
STMformer contains four key components:IMM, SMM, TMM-TB,
TMM-PCA. To prove that the key modules can help the STMformer
to mine spatio-temporal feature of data, we designed five variants of
the model. These variants were compared against the whole STM-
former, with sharing identical hyperparameters. The descriptions
of these five variants are as follows:

• w/o SMM: This model variant removes the SMM. It is utilized

instances.
• w/o TMM-TB: This model variant removes the TB module
of TMM, serving to demonstrate the necessity of learning
the trends in its own time series variations.

instances. Removing the IMM leads to a significant increase in pre-
diction errors. This is because a noticeable change in the state of
the host or one of its instances can disrupt the operation of other
instances. (2) Dynamic adjacency matrices significantly impact sys-
tem state predictions. Removing the SMM also increases errors.
This is because variations in TCP connection events at each time
step can alter the dependencies among instances, thereby affecting
their states. Removing this module would omit the transmission
of spatial information within single time step. (3) Removing TMM-
TB would increase prediction errors. The primary reason is that
the variables have hidden trends within the time series that follow
certain patterns, which are not solely influenced by spatial relation-
ships. This highlights the necessity to account for time-intrinsic
fluctuation in addition to spatial interactions. (4) Calculating the
impact of cascading effects from a global perspective aids in system
state prediction. After the removal of the TMM-PCA, an increase
in prediction errors was observed. Computing attention from a
global spatio-temporal perspective effectively captures the state
transmission between multi-hop nodes and over long time intervals.
This approach highlights the necessity of incorporating a global
analysis to understand and predict the dynamics across the network
of interconnected services more accurately.
4.6 Hyperparameter Studies
Changes in the hyperparameters of the STMformer typically affect
model’s predictive performance. To validate the impact of hyperpa-
rameters on the STMformer, we will analyze from five perspectives:
the dimension of the model, the choice of kernel length for sequence
decomposition, the number of attention heads, the ProbSparseAt-
tention factor, and the hyperparameters of the TB-PCA module.
As the Fig. 4(a) shows, changes in model parameters significantly
affect the performance of the STMformer. As the dimensions of
model parameters increase, the performance of the model improves.
This indicates that a higher-dimensional vector space enhances the
model’s learning capabilities. Node states, after being processed
through various spatio-temporal relationship calculations, implic-
itly contain elements of physical spatial deployment, spatial logical
relationships, trends in time series, and global spatio-temporal re-
lationships. Enhancing model parameters helps nodes learn these
complex features. Fig. 4(b) illustrates that the model is influenced
by the choice of kernel for sequence decomposition. The optimal
selection of kernel length depends on the pattern fluctuations of
the time series and expert experience. Choosing the appropriate
set of kernel lengths can more accurately obtain trends, allowing
the model to focus on learning the remaining parts of the series.
The Fig. 4(c) and Fig. 4(d) display experiments related to attention-
related hyperparameters. The choice of the number of attention
heads, if too large or too small, affects the model’s performance,
=== page 10 ===
Conference’24, July, 2024 Yifei Xu et al.
as it influences the model’s ability to parallelize learning across
different aspects of the data, potentially leading to either redundant
learning or insufficient feature capture. Regarding the selection
of the ProbSparseAttention factor, it is evident that its impact on
model performance is not significant. This is because, in the context
of instance states, only a small portion of the variables are affected.
ProbSparseAttention consistently selects the variables with the
highest associations, ensuring that the most critical features are
always considered.
The Fig. 4(e) and Fig. 4(f) indicate that higher dimensions of ran-
dom feature mapping and more sampling times of Gumbel-Softmax
correlate with improved model performance. Increasing the dimen-
sionality of mapping means that spatio-temporal information can be
better represented in another vector space. Meanwhile, increasing
the number of sampling times means that the operation’s frequency
is higher, ensuring more accurate approximation of the softmax
distribution. Although these two hyperparameters increase compu-
tation time, such a trade-off is acceptable compared to the benefits
of achieving better model performance.
5 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
For predicting the state of microservices systems, we developed the
STMformer model, which leverages dynamically derived adjacency
matrices from network events and deployment structures to cap-
ture spatio-temporal relationships characteristic of microservices
systems. We also design PatchCrossAttention module to analyze
cascading effects from a global spatio-temporal perspective. Our ex-
periments show that STMformer outperforms benchmark methods,
confirming the effectiveness of its components and the influence of
hyperparameters on its performance. Our future work will focus on
reducing computational complexity, automating kernel generation
for sequence decomposition, and integrating multimodal data for
more robust microservices system representations.

# STMformer (Xu et al., arXiv 2024)

> Notes from the **full text** (`litdb/texts/yifeixu...txt`). Page numbers are PDF pages. Figs 1-4 not inspected.

## 1. Summary
A transformer model that forecasts metric time series of microservice pods using three message modules: same-host interactions (IMM), a graph attention network over per-step TCP-connection adjacency matrices (SMM), and a temporal module combining TimesNet blocks with a global patch cross-attention that is meant to capture cascading effects. Evaluated on one Train-Ticket deployment with six injected fault types, against six time-series and two spatio-temporal baselines.

## 2. Problem and motivation
- Forecasting system states helps AIOps tasks; microservice states depend on host co-location, call connections and delayed cascading effects (pp.1-2). Fig 1(b) shows one example of delayed CPU fluctuation in a neighbour after a fault. Evidence: one demonstration, not a rate.

## 3. Method (pp.4-6)
Series decomposition, embedding, one-stride patching; encoder with IMM, SMM, TMM (TimesBlock plus PatchCrossAttention mixed by a random matrix alpha, Eq 6); global spatio-temporal adjacency from STSGT; ProbSparse attention. Time-varying adjacency from eBPF-observed TCP connection latency and frequency.

## 4. Data and setup (pp.6-8)
- Own collector (coroot-node-agent based), 80+ metrics, 5-second sampling, 1-2 hours per condition, 41-service Train-Ticket on seven VMs, Locust load, six Chaos Mesh faults (p.6).
- Split 8:1:1, horizon equals prediction length, 16 and 32 (short) and 64 and 128 (long) steps (p.8).
- Whether windows are split by time or at random is not stated; overlapping windows from one run with a random split would leak.

## 5. Results (copied)
| Task | Metric | Theirs | Best baseline | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Short, step 16 | MAE / MSE | 0.01663 / 0.002102 | FEDformer 0.01709 MAE; PatchTST 0.002126 MSE | Table 1 p.7 |
| Short, step 32 | MAE / MSE | 0.01623 / 0.002084 | TimesNet 0.01684 MAE; PatchTST 0.002135 MSE | Table 1 |
| Long, step 64 | MAE / MSE | 0.01644 / 0.002040 | PatchTST 0.01899 MAE; 0.002053 MSE | Table 2 p.8 |
| Long, step 128 | MAE / MSE | 0.01728 / 0.002126 | TimesNet 0.01818 MAE; PatchTST 0.002081 MSE (PatchTST better) | Table 2 |
| Ablation (step 64) | MAE | 0.01644 | w/o PCA 0.04434; w/o IMM 0.5768 | Table 3 p.8 |

## 6. Limitations
- Stated: computational cost, kernel selection, single modality (p.10).
- **My critique:**
  1. Task is metric forecasting; no evaluation of whether it predicts faults, anomalies or cascades earlier than a threshold on the raw series. The word "cascading effects" refers to a modelling module, not a measured outcome.
  2. The abstract's 8.6% MAE and 2.2% MSE gains do not match the tables I can compute: step 16 MAE gain over FEDformer is about 2.7% and MSE gain over PatchTST about 1.1%; at step 128 PatchTST has lower MSE (0.002081 vs 0.002126). The abstract numbers may be averages of specific cells; the paper does not show the calculation.
  3. Table 3's "w/o IMM" has MAE 0.5768 but RMSE 0.1300; MAE cannot exceed RMSE, so at least one number is wrong (as printed in the PDF text).
  4. No persistence baseline (predict last value) or seasonal naive baseline, which are strong when errors are around 0.017 on min-max scaled data.
  5. Random matrix alpha in Eq 6 is described as a "uniform random matrix"; the role is not justified.
  6. One deployment, one split, no repeated seeds or intervals; the STSGT baseline does not converge in some settings (p.8), so the spatio-temporal baselines are weak.

## 7. Reproducibility
- Code stated at github.com/xuyifeiiie/STMformer (not checked). Dataset not stated as released.

| Dimension | This paper | Ours (rca-lab) | Who is stronger, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Label requirement | none for training | none | tie |
| Live / streaming | offline windows | incremental windows | ours (claimed) |
| Telemetry used | eBPF metrics, TCP connections | traces (+ metrics) | theirs richer |
| Propagation modelling | dynamic adjacency + host co-location + attention | call-edge probabilities | theirs includes co-location |
| Forecasts future failures | no (forecasts metrics) | claimed | n/a |
| Explanation | none | templates | ours |
| Evaluation rigor | one run, no naive baseline | synthetic | neither |
| Open / reproducible | code stated | yes | tie |

- "STMformer combines same-host attention, TCP-connection-based dynamic graphs and cross-time attention for pod metric forecasting on Train-Ticket" (pp.3-6).
- "Ablating the host-interaction module (IMM) or the connection module (SMM) increased error in the authors' ablation (Table 3 p.8), but Table 3 contains an inconsistent MAE/RMSE pair."

- Split protocol; whether the dataset is public; published version (if any).

# Batch 08: 2026-10-08

Papers: 1) AID (Yang et al., arXiv 2021), 2) Unyi et al. (IEEE TNSM 2025, GNN fault forecasting), 3) STMformer (Xu et al., arXiv 2024).
All read in full: yes (figures not inspected; Unyi Table III values and Table I did not extract).
Scopus: AID and STMformer are arXiv preprints (not Scopus-indexed); TNSM ISSN 1932-4537 not yet checked in the Scopus preview. SJR quartiles unknown (no list supplied; please add a Scopus or Scimago file to `litdb/reference/`).
Note: these three PDFs came from arXiv and an institutional repository (open access) via `litdb/tools/fetch_oa.py`, with your permission.

## 1. Side-by-side
| | AID | Unyi et al. | STMformer | Ours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Type | method (edge strength) | method (simulation) | method (metric forecasting) | RCA + untested risk |
| Task | dependency intensity from traces | graph-level fault probability regression | pod metric forecasting | RCA + cascade risk |
| Labels | none (labels for eval) | simulator labels | none | none |
| Telemetry | traces | none | eBPF metrics + TCP connections | traces (+ metrics, SSH) |
| Propagation | time-warped caller/callee similarity | GNN on retry/MDP model | GAT + attention + host grouping | edge probabilities |
| Forecasting | no | no (aggregate formula) | metric values only | claimed, untested |
| Data (open?) | stated, unchecked | synthetic, stated, unchecked | own, dataset not stated | open |
| Headline | Industry CE 0.327 vs 0.603 | R2 0.99 on synthetic | MAE 0.0166 vs 0.0171 (step 16) | none on real faults |
| Evidence quality | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 |

## 2. What each means for our claims
- **AID:** closest to our edge-weight learning: label-free, trace-based, evaluated against 94 hand-labelled edges. It does not forecast. Our edge-probability estimator must be compared with its DSW similarity; the 89% strong labels mean a constant predictor is a necessary baseline.
- **Unyi et al.:** "GNN fault forecasting" that is simulation-only and regresses a model-checker output from its own inputs. It cannot be used as evidence that cascade risk is predictable from real telemetry.
- **STMformer:** forecasts metric values; uses host co-location and TCP connection graphs. Supports our limitation that call-edge-only propagation misses co-location. Its abstract gains do not match its tables, and Table 3 has an impossible MAE/RMSE pair.

## 3. Does this batch change the problem statement?
- Real? AID reports five of 13 public AWS outages as dependency-related (Table I p.4) and engineer interviews at one company; thin but consistent.
- Already solved? Less than assumed: none of the three forecasts real failures or cascades from telemetry. Label-free edge strength from traces is covered (AID).
- Misframed? Our claim should be "label-free, trace-based cascade-risk scoring with calibrated evaluation", not "first to learn edge strength".

## 4. Baselines and datasets to add because of this batch
- AID (github.com/OpsPAI/aid): propagation-weight baseline (DSW similarity per call edge), and its released TT dataset with 19 labelled edges.
- A constant "strong" predictor and a persistence baseline for forecasting tasks (reporting hygiene seen missing here).
- Check STMformer repo and dataset availability before citing the dataset.

## 5. Claims in our draft that this batch contradicts or weakens
- Any claim that learning call-edge strength without labels is new (AID).
- Any claim that GNN fault forecasting exists for real telemetry (Unyi is synthetic only).

## 6. Sentences we can safely write (with citation keys)
- "AID estimates continuous dependency intensity from traces without labels [tianyiyang...2021efficient]."
- "Forecasting models that use host co-location and connection graphs exist [yifeixu...2024system]; they forecast metrics, not failures."
- "A GNN has been trained to predict model-checker fault probabilities on synthetic service meshes [unyi2025explainable]; real-trace evaluation is future work (p.16)."
- Do NOT write: AID's 45.8% / 61.1% / 33.2% as general performance; STMformer's 8.6% / 2.2%; Unyi's R2 values as evidence of forecasting.

## 7. Corrections needed to earlier notes or reports
1. `docs/REVIEW_REPORT.md` section 3.2 (checked by abstract only): AID "predicts cascading impact via dependency intensity" is imprecise: it predicts the dependency intensity value (edge strength); it does not forecast failure impact or time.
2. REVIEW_REPORT's IEEE TNSM 2025 entry ("GNN fault forecasting with probabilistic propagation") is a simulation-only paper with synthetic labels; it is weaker prior art than assumed.
3. PROBLEM_EVIDENCE.md section B row 1 (AID: "predicts cascading impact via dependency intensity") and row 2 (TNSM 2025) should be read with these corrections; updated in this batch.

## 8. Proposals (no code changed)
- Add a per-edge AID-style DSW similarity as an alternative edge weight and compare to our learned weights on RCAEval.
- Report a constant-prediction baseline and ECE/Brier for any risk output.

- Own collector (coroot-node-agent based), 80+ metrics, 5-second sampling, 1-2 hours per condition, 41-service Train-Ticket on seven VMs, Locust load, six Chaos Mesh faults (p.6).
- Split 8:1:1, horizon equals prediction length, 16 and 32 (short) and 64 and 128 (long) steps (p.8).
- Whether windows are split by time or at random is not stated; overlapping windows from one run with a random split would leak.

## 5. Results (copied)
| Task | Metric | Theirs | Best baseline | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Short, step 16 | MAE / MSE | 0.01663 / 0.002102 | FEDformer 0.01709 MAE; PatchTST 0.002126 MSE | Table 1 p.7 |
| Short, step 32 | MAE / MSE | 0.01623 / 0.002084 | TimesNet 0.01684 MAE; PatchTST 0.002135 MSE | Table 1 |
| Long, step 64 | MAE / MSE | 0.01644 / 0.002040 | PatchTST 0.01899 MAE; 0.002053 MSE | Table 2 p.8 |
| Long, step 128 | MAE / MSE | 0.01728 / 0.002126 | TimesNet 0.01818 MAE; PatchTST 0.002081 MSE (PatchTST better) | Table 2 |
| Ablation (step 64) | MAE | 0.01644 | w/o PCA 0.04434; w/o IMM 0.5768 | Table 3 p.8 |

## 6. Limitations
- Stated: computational cost, kernel selection, single modality (p.10).
- **My critique:**
  1. Task is metric forecasting; no evaluation of whether it predicts faults, anomalies or cascades earlier than a threshold on the raw series. The word "cascading effects" refers to a modelling module, not a measured outcome.
  2. The abstract's 8.6% MAE and 2.2% MSE gains do not match the tables I can compute: step 16 MAE gain over FEDformer is about 2.7% and MSE gain over PatchTST about 1.1%; at step 128 PatchTST has lower MSE (0.002081 vs 0.002126). The abstract numbers may be averages of specific cells; the paper does not show the calculation.
  3. Table 3's "w/o IMM" has MAE 0.5768 but RMSE 0.1300; MAE cannot exceed RMSE, so at least one number is wrong (as printed in the PDF text).
  4. No persistence baseline (predict last value) or seasonal naive baseline, which are strong when errors are around 0.017 on min-max scaled data.
  5. Random matrix alpha in Eq 6 is described as a "uniform random matrix"; the role is not justified.
  6. One deployment, one split, no repeated seeds or intervals; the STSGT baseline does not converge in some settings (p.8), so the spatio-temporal baselines are weak.
  7. Dataset release is not stated; the PDF carries a placeholder ACM DOI and conference name.
- Not discussed: leakage from overlapping windows, performance specifically around fault periods.

## 7. Reproducibility
- Code stated at github.com/xuyifeiiie/STMformer (not checked). Dataset not stated as released.

## 8. Comparison with OUR work
| Dimension | This paper | Ours (rca-lab) | Who is stronger, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Label requirement | none for training | none | tie |
| Live / streaming | offline windows | incremental windows | ours (claimed) |
| Telemetry used | eBPF metrics, TCP connections | traces (+ metrics) | theirs richer |
| Propagation modelling | dynamic adjacency + host co-location + attention | call-edge probabilities | theirs includes co-location |
| Forecasts future failures | no (forecasts metrics) | claimed | n/a |
| Explanation | none | templates | ours |
| Evaluation rigor | one run, no naive baseline | synthetic | neither |
| Open / reproducible | code stated | yes | tie |

- **What they have that we do not:** host co-location and connection-level dynamic adjacency as inputs.
- **What we have that they do not:** RCA output and a risk score tied to edges.
- **Could a reviewer say "this already exists"?** For "forecast pod metrics using call and co-location structure": yes. Not for cascade-risk scoring.
- **Position:** supports our limitation that call edges alone miss co-location effects; cite as forecasting prior art that uses host co-location.
- **Must we run it as a baseline?** No.

## 9. Does this paper change what problem we should solve?
- Slightly: it shows co-location (same host) is treated as a propagation channel in forecasting, which our call-edge model omits.

## 10. Citation-ready facts (each with page)
- "STMformer combines same-host attention, TCP-connection-based dynamic graphs and cross-time attention for pod metric forecasting on Train-Ticket" (pp.3-6).
- "Ablating the host-interaction module (IMM) or the connection module (SMM) increased error in the authors' ablation (Table 3 p.8), but Table 3 contains an inconsistent MAE/RMSE pair."

## 11. Open questions / things to verify
- Split protocol; whether the dataset is public; published version (if any).
